companies.name: AST SpaceMobile, Inc.

reports.title: AST SpaceMobile ER101
reports.summary: A pre-commercial infrastructure bet. AST has the partner list (60+ carriers, ~3 billion subscribers), $1.3bn of contracted revenue and >$3.7bn of pro forma liquidity, but only 13 of the ~45-60 satellites it needs for continuous service. At ~$17bn EV the market is paying for a working network in 2027, while a launch failure in April, Falcon 9 dependence and SpaceX's spectrum land-grab have halved the stock in a year. Consensus sits at Hold with targets of $42.50 to $108.

companies.name: Lennar Corporation

reports.title: Lennar (LEN) | Equity Research 101
reports.summary: Lennar is the second-largest US homebuilder by deliveries (82,583 homes in FY2025). It buys or options land, builds mostly entry-level and first move-up single-family homes (average price about $372,000 in Q3 FY2026) in roughly two dozen states, and sells them with an 'Everything's Included' feature package. It earns a second, smaller profit pool by writing the mortgage and title policy for most of its own buyers. Since 2025 it runs a 'land-light' model: it owns under 2.5% of about 488,000 homesites it controls, renting land via option contracts (largely with Millrose Properties, spun off in 2025) and paying for lots only when it is ready to build.

Source: Anthropic (ANT) 101 (2026-11-22) · open in site

Equity research 101 · Nasdaq: ANT · USD · price as of Nov 20, 2026 close

Anthropic: the fastest revenue ramp ever listed, priced for years more of it

Quarterly revenue went from $0.4bn to $17.0bn in six quarters and the business now makes an adjusted profit. At about 26x trailing sales (net of cash) the market is paying for consensus 2027 revenue of roughly $128bn, against $901bn of compute commitments.

Takeaways

Method and sources

1. What it does and how it makes money

Anthropic, PBC builds the Claude family of AI models and sells access to them. It is a public benefit corporation, founded in January 2021 by seven former OpenAI researchers led by Dario and Daniela Amodei.

Two revenue streams. Consumption: businesses and developers pay per token (unit of text processed) through the API and through cloud marketplaces. Subscriptions: monthly Claude plans for individuals and teams, plus Claude Code, its agentic coding product.

In the first nine months of 2026, consumption revenue grew by $24.2bn and subscriptions by $6.5bn, so roughly four fifths of the growth came from usage-based selling to businesses.

A model lab that sells mostly to businesses, not consumers. Revenue grew from $41m (2023) to $35.3bn TTM, and usage-based API revenue is the engine, so revenue tracks how much work customers hand to Claude.

How it got here

Jan 2021

Founded by seven ex-OpenAI researchers as a public benefit corporation.

2023

First Claude models released; revenue $41m for the year.

Jun 2024

Claude 3.5 Sonnet starts a long run at the top of coding benchmarks. 2024 revenue $386m.

Feb to May 2025

Claude Code launched, then generally available with Claude 4.

Sep 2025

Series F at $183bn. $1.5bn Bartz copyright settlement booked. 2025 revenue $4.6bn.

Feb 2026

Series G at $380bn. Pentagon names Anthropic a supply-chain risk; lawsuit filed in March.

Q2 2026

First quarterly GAAP operating profit ($974m). Series H-1 raises $45.7bn.

Oct 26, 2026

S-1 filed; amended Nov 2 with Q3 results.

Nov 19, 2026

Lists on Nasdaq at $83, the largest IPO on record; closes day one at $97.17.

2. Moat: why it earns its returns, and can rivals copy it?

Real advantages

Coding and agent leadership. Menlo Ventures put Claude at 54% of enterprise coding spend vs 21% for OpenAI (Dec 2025), and estimates Claude Code plus OpenAI's Codex take 70% of a $34bn AI coding market (Nov 2026).

Enterprise trust. Anthropic's share of enterprise LLM API spend rose from 12% in 2023 to 40% (Menlo, Dec 2025). Over 1,900 customers pay $1m+ a year; about 250 pay $10m+.

Workflow lock-in. Net revenue retention of about 900%: customers who were paying a year ago now pay about 9x more. Agents built around one model family are costly to re-test and re-tune.

Capital and compute access. $141bn raised before the IPO, plus a $26bn strategic placement from Google, NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC.

What is copyable

Model leads decay fast. Frontier capability gaps have historically closed within months; OpenAI, Google and open-weight models compete on every release.

Low switching cost at the API level. Swapping a model endpoint is cheap; the lock-in sits in tooling, evals and agents, not contracts.

Price. Analysts cited by The Next Web found businesses hitting AI budget limits and some moving to cheaper models.

The moat is real but young: leadership in coding and agents, plus deep enterprise adoption (NRR ~900%). It rests on staying at the frontier each model cycle, which is a capability race funded by compute, not a structural lock like a network effect.

3. Drivers: what revenue is made of

Revenue = tokens used x price per token x model mix + seats x subscription price. Volume is the engine: every new model release (Claude 4 in May 2025 onward) has lifted usage per customer. Price per token tends to fall each generation, so growth depends on usage rising faster than price falls.

KPI that moves it Latest Why it matters

Run-rate revenue $81bn (Oct 31, 2026) Best real-time read of the top line; Q3 annualised is ~$68bn.

Customers paying $1m+ a year 1,900+ Breadth of large enterprise adoption.

Customers paying $100k+ 11,900+ (74% of revenue) Up from ~400 in Mar 2025; concentration check.

Net revenue retention ~900% Expansion inside existing accounts.

Compute cost growth vs revenue growth 382% vs 1,127% YoY Whether scale is improving unit economics.

Watch run-rate revenue and $1m+ customer count first; then compute cost as a share of revenue. If revenue keeps outgrowing compute (1,127% vs 382% YoY in Q3) the margin story holds.

Growth deceleration is already visible. QoQ growth fell from 144% in Q2 to 47% in Q3. Run-rate grew about 4-5% a month into October by one forecaster's reading.

Price war and model commoditisation. Cheaper models from OpenAI, Google and open-weight labs compress price per token.

Government conflict. The Defense Department labelled Anthropic a supply-chain risk in Feb 2026 after it refused autonomous-weapons and mass-surveillance uses; litigation is ongoing.

Dilution and lock-ups. 1.77bn options and 1.13bn RSUs sit on 13.2bn shares; about $14.2bn of RSU expense is recognised on the IPO. Some 3.7bn shares can be sold before the 180-day lock-up ends.

Method, glossary and sources

Metric definitions

Revenue growth: reported. Anthropic does not disclose organic growth; acquisitions are small (goodwill $595m), so reported is used as an estimate of organic.

Operating margin: GAAP operating income / revenue; adjusted figure is the company's non-GAAP measure.

NOPAT: operating income x (1 - 21% normalised US tax); losses carry no tax shield because none is recognised.

Invested capital: total assets minus cash and short-term investments, minus operating liabilities (total liabilities less convertible notes and lease liabilities). Dec 31, 2025: $781m; Sep 30, 2026: $10,778m; average $5,780m. Restricted cash kept in. This excludes ~$901bn of off-balance-sheet compute commitments, so ROIC and sales/capital overstate economic returns.

ROIC: annualised quarterly or TTM NOPAT / average invested capital. Incremental ROIC: change in annualised adjusted NOPAT (Q3 2026 vs Q4 2025) / change in invested capital; noisy.

FCF: operating cash flow minus purchases of property and equipment. Finance-leased equipment ($1.7bn of finance lease liabilities) is not in capex, so FCF flatters slightly.

FCF conversion: FCF / adjusted NOPAT (GAAP NOPAT is negative).

Net debt / EBITDA: not meaningful; net cash. Pro forma net cash = Sep 30 cash and STI $131.8bn + ~$116bn net proceeds from 1.103bn Class A and 0.313bn Class N shares at $83 (gross $117.6bn, fees estimated) - $4.5bn lease liabilities. Estimate.

Q3 SBC estimated as nine-month SBC ($3,255m) less first-half SBC (~$2.2bn).

Diluted shares: 13.22bn basic + 1.77bn options + 1.13bn RSUs (S-1/A, Sep 30). Broader fully diluted counts reported in press are ~18bn.

1. What it does and how it makes money

Anthropic, PBC builds the Claude family of AI models and sells access to them. It is a public benefit corporation, founded in January 2021 by seven former OpenAI researchers led by Dario and Daniela Amodei.

Two revenue streams. Consumption: businesses and developers pay per token (unit of text processed) through the API and through cloud marketplaces. Subscriptions: monthly Claude plans for individuals and teams, plus Claude Code, its agentic coding product.

In the first nine months of 2026, consumption revenue grew by $24.2bn and subscriptions by $6.5bn, so roughly four fifths of the growth came from usage-based selling to businesses.

A model lab that sells mostly to businesses, not consumers. Revenue grew from $41m (2023) to $35.3bn TTM, and usage-based API revenue is the engine, so revenue tracks how much work customers hand to Claude.

2. Moat: why it earns its returns, and can rivals copy it?
Real advantages
Coding and agent leadership. Menlo Ventures put Claude at 54% of enterprise coding spend vs 21% for OpenAI (Dec 2025), and estimates Claude Code plus OpenAI's Codex take 70% of a $34bn AI coding market (Nov 2026).
Enterprise trust. Anthropic's share of enterprise LLM API spend rose from 12% in 2023 to 40% (Menlo, Dec 2025). Over 1,900 customers pay $1m+ a year; about 250 pay $10m+.
Workflow lock-in. Net revenue retention of about 900%: customers who were paying a year ago now pay about 9x more. Agents built around one model family are costly to re-test and re-tune.
Capital and compute access. $141bn raised before the IPO, plus a $26bn strategic placement from Google, NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC.
What is copyable
Model leads decay fast. Frontier capability gaps have historically closed within months; OpenAI, Google and open-weight models compete on every release.
Low switching cost at the API level. Swapping a model endpoint is cheap; the lock-in sits in tooling, evals and agents, not contracts.
Price. Analysts cited by The Next Web found businesses hitting AI budget limits and some moving to cheaper models.
The moat is real but young: leadership in coding and agents, plus deep enterprise adoption (NRR ~900%). It rests on staying at the frontier each model cycle, which is a capability race funded by compute, not a structural lock like a network effect.
3. Drivers: what revenue is made of

Revenue = tokens used x price per token x model mix + seats x subscription price. Volume is the engine: every new model release (Claude 4 in May 2025 onward) has lifted usage per customer. Price per token tends to fall each generation, so growth depends on usage rising faster than price falls.

Check next
Q4 2026 results: QoQ growth vs 47% in Q3, and the ~$14.2bn RSU charge.
Compute and infrastructure as % of revenue (48% Q2, 58% Q3).
Run-rate revenue updates and $1m+ customer count.
Pentagon litigation outcome and lock-up expiry dates.
OpenAI pricing moves and any OpenAI S-1 for a direct comparison.
Method, glossary and sources
Metric definitions
Revenue growth: reported. Anthropic does not disclose organic growth; acquisitions are small (goodwill $595m), so reported is used as an estimate of organic.
Operating margin: GAAP operating income / revenue; adjusted figure is the company's non-GAAP measure.
NOPAT: operating income x (1 - 21% normalised US tax); losses carry no tax shield because none is recognised.
Invested capital: total assets minus cash and short-term investments, minus operating liabilities (total liabilities less convertible notes and lease liabilities). Dec 31, 2025: $781m; Sep 30, 2026: $10,778m; average $5,780m. Restricted cash kept in. This excludes ~$901bn of off-balance-sheet compute commitments, so ROIC and sales/capital overstate economic returns.
ROIC: annualised quarterly or TTM NOPAT / average invested capital. Incremental ROIC: change in annualised adjusted NOPAT (Q3 2026 vs Q4 2025) / change in invested capital; noisy.
FCF: operating cash flow minus purchases of property and equipment. Finance-leased equipment ($1.7bn of finance lease liabilities) is not in capex, so FCF flatters slightly.
FCF conversion: FCF / adjusted NOPAT (GAAP NOPAT is negative).
Net debt / EBITDA: not meaningful; net cash. Pro forma net cash = Sep 30 cash and STI $131.8bn + ~$116bn net proceeds from 1.103bn Class A and 0.313bn Class N shares at $83 (gross $117.6bn, fees estimated) - $4.5bn lease liabilities. Estimate.
Q3 SBC estimated as nine-month SBC ($3,255m) less first-half SBC (~$2.2bn).
Diluted shares: 13.22bn basic + 1.77bn options + 1.13bn RSUs (S-1/A, Sep 30). Broader fully diluted counts reported in press are ~18bn.
Glossary
Sources

What does it do, and how did it get here?

TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker. It manufactures chips designed by others (Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Broadcom, Qualcomm and hundreds more) and, increasingly, packages them together with its CoWoS advanced packaging. It does not sell chips under its own name, so it never competes with its customers.

Business model

Customers buy processed silicon wafers. Price per wafer rises steeply with each new process node, so revenue grows through more wafers, higher prices and a richer node mix. The cost base is mostly depreciation on fabs and tools, which makes margins very sensitive to utilisation.

1987Founded by Morris Chang in Hsinchu as the world's first dedicated (pure-play) foundry.

Reading: TSMC sells manufacturing capacity, not chips. Three in four wafer dollars now come from 7nm and better, and AI/HPC is 68% of revenue, so this is effectively the factory for the AI build-out.

02

Why does it earn its returns, and can anyone copy it?

PROCESS LEADERSHIP

3nm and 2nm volume first, with yields rivals have not matched. 79% of wafer revenue is 7nm or better.

SCALE ECONOMICS

Capex of US$60-64bn in 2026; only 2 rivals even attempt the leading edge. Spreading R&D (NT$230bn in 9M26) over 72.5% share is the cost advantage.

SWITCHING COSTS

A chip design is tied to one foundry's process kit; porting a leading-edge design costs years and hundreds of millions of dollars.

TRUSTED NEUTRALITY

No own-brand chips, so Apple, Nvidia and AMD can share the same factory without fear of competition.

ECOSYSTEM

Design libraries, EDA partners (Open Innovation Platform) and CoWoS packaging lock in the AI supply chain.

COPY TEST

Intel Foundry loses about US$2.5bn a quarter and Samsung Foundry sits near break-even with 5.9% share: well-funded rivals have tried and failed to close the gap.

Reading: The moat is scale plus learning: TSMC spends more on leading-edge capacity in one year (US$60-64bn in 2026) than most rivals are worth, and it gets yields right first. Its 72.5% share of foundry revenue is the scoreboard.

03

What is revenue made of?

Revenue = wafers shipped × price per wafer × node mix, plus advanced packaging. In 3Q26 the node mix was 2nm 8%, 3nm 33%, 5nm 28%, 7nm 10%, 16nm and older 21% of wafer revenue.

Top-10 foundry revenue reached a record US$53.5bn in 2Q26 (+11.5% QoQ, TrendForce), and Counterpoint puts pure-play foundry growth at 29% YoY. TSMC took 72.5% of it. Who runs it, and how do they spend the cash?

C.C. Wei

Wendell Huang

Ownership

Directors and officers hold 60.2m shares, 0.23% (Feb 2026). Largest holder: Taiwan's National Development Fund, 6.38%. ADR holders 20.5%.

Stated plan

Capture AI demand ("no intention to leave food on the table"), keep long-term gross margin at 56% or higher and ROE in the high-20s through the cycle, build 2nm/A16 in Taiwan and Arizona.

Recent signal

Director Michael Splinter bought 840 ADRs at US$357 on 5 Nov 2026 (small, but a buy).

Capital allocation, last 12 months

Capex: NT$1,647bn TTM (33% of revenue); 2026 budget raised twice to US$60-64bn; a further US$40.9bn appropriated on 10 Nov 2026.

Dividends: NT$571bn paid TTM (+29% YoY). Quarterly dividend raised from NT$7 to a record NT$9 per share for 3Q26. Policy: annual dividend never below the prior year.

Buybacks: none. Share count flat at 25.93bn.

M&A: none material. New: up to US$500m each into Anthropic (at IPO) and OpenAI preferred stock, plus a US$500m strategic investment vehicle.

Overseas: Arizona plan raised to US$265bn (about 30% of 2nm-and-below capacity eventually), Kumamoto Fab 2, Dresden JV.

Reading: A professional, engineer-led team with low personal ownership (directors and officers hold 0.23%) but a clear, consistent playbook: reinvest heavily, raise the dividend every year, no buybacks, no big acquisitions.

08

What would break the story?

RISK SEVERITY WHAT WOULD HAPPEN SIGNAL TO WATCH

AI capex digestion High Hyperscaler spending pauses; 2026-28 capex already committed leaves idle tools. Wei: 2027 planning is "prudent". Monthly revenue, Nvidia/hyperscaler capex guides

Customer concentration High Nvidia ~22% of 2026 sales (JPMorgan est.). Nvidia's CEO change and AI-financing worries cut TSMC ~6% on 16 Nov 2026. Nvidia orders, CoWoS bookings

Taiwan geopolitics Low prob., severe Most leading-edge capacity sits in Taiwan; a blockade or conflict would impair the core asset. Cross-strait news; Arizona ramp

Margin dilution Medium Overseas fabs cut gross margin 2-3 pts early, 3-4 pts later; 2nm ramp dilutes 3-4 pts in 2H26. GM vs 56% long-term floor

Policy and tariffs Medium Possible US tariffs on imported chips, export controls (China was 5.5% of 3Q26 revenue), CHIPS-style conditions. US trade actions

FX Medium A stronger NT$ cuts reported NT$ revenue and gross margin; 4Q26 guidance assumes NT$31.8/US$. USD/TWD vs 31.8 guide rate

Competition Low-medium Intel 18A/14A and Samsung 2nm win a large AI or Apple-scale order. Major customer wins at rivals

Reading: The business risk is cyclical (AI digestion after record capex), the tail risk is geopolitical (Taiwan). The November 2026 sell-off around Nvidia shows how much of the story rides on one customer's demand.

1. Business overview

What does it do, how does it make money, and how did it get here?

Lennar is the second-largest US homebuilder by deliveries (82,583 homes in FY2025). It buys or options land, builds mostly entry-level and first move-up single-family homes (average price about $372,000 in Q3 FY2026) in roughly two dozen states, and sells them with an 'Everything's Included' feature package. It earns a second, smaller profit pool by writing the mortgage and title policy for most of its own buyers. Since 2025 it runs a 'land-light' model: it owns under 2.5% of about 488,000 homesites it controls, renting land via option contracts (largely with Millrose Properties, spun off in 2025) and paying for lots only when it is ready to build.

Timeline

Read: Over 95% of revenue and essentially all of the profit come from building and selling homes. Lennar is a manufacturing-and-sales machine for starter homes, not a land speculator any more, which is the point of the 2025 Millrose spin-off.

2. Moat

Why does it earn its returns, and can competitors copy it?

Real advantages

Scale on cost: construction costs down about 12-13% over two years and cycle time at a record low (116 days in Q3 FY26 per company commentary). Volume gives buying power with trades and suppliers that small builders lack.

Land-light balance sheet: controlling about 98% of lots by option means less capital tied up in dirt and lower write-down risk, which should lift asset turns once margins normalise.

Captive mortgage and title: Financial Services earned $323M in 9M FY26 (on $679M revenue) and lets Lennar fund rate buydowns that smaller rivals cannot match.

Standardised, even-flow production ('Everything's Included', limited options) keeps the factory running at a steady pace.

What limits the moat

Homes are a near-commodity: buyers compare on price and payment, and existing-home sellers now compete directly in Lennar's price bands.

The volume-first strategy hands margin to the customer: incentives of about 12-14% of price in FY26 versus a 4-6% 'normal' level.

Peers (D.R. Horton, NVR, PulteGroup) have the same scale or the same option-land model and earn far higher margins and ROIC today.

Option land is not free: lot option fees to land bankers are a cost that sits inside gross margin.

Read: The moat is cost and scale, not pricing power. That is a real but narrow advantage: it lets Lennar survive a downturn and keep volume, but the current numbers show it does not let Lennar keep margin. Moat strength: moderate, cyclical.

6. Industry and competitors

Is the industry growing, and how does Lennar stack up?

Near term, weak: NAHB/Wells Fargo builder confidence fell to 25 in Nov 2026, lowest since April 2012; 46% of builders cut prices and 68% used incentives. 30-year mortgage rates are cited around 7-7.5%.

Margins compressing across the group: Q3 gross margins, Lennar 15.8% (from 17.5%), KB Home 16.5%, Meritage 17.4%, Toll 23.9%, PulteGroup 24.8%. D.R. Horton guides FY27 closings flat to down 6% and Q1 FY27 margin to 18-18.5%.

Long run, supportive: the US has under-built homes for over a decade and existing owners are locked into low-rate mortgages, so new homes take an outsized share of sales once affordability improves. Growth prospects hinge on rates, not on demand for shelter.

Structure: the top builders keep gaining share from small private builders who lack cheap capital, mortgage arms and land options.

Read: The industry is in a demand trough with a long-run supply shortage behind it. Lennar ranks last of five large peers on operating margin and ROIC yet trades at the highest P/E and EV/EBIT. Investors pay for its recovery potential, not its current returns.

7. Management

Who runs it, what do they plan, how much do they own, how do they allocate capital?

CEO

Stuart Miller: Executive Chairman, CEO and President. With Lennar since 1982, CEO 1997-2018, Executive Chairman since 2018, Co-CEO from 2023, sole CEO since Jan 2026.

CFO

Diane Bessette, CFO since 2019.

Ownership

Miller beneficially owns about 2.4M Class A and 21.9M Class B shares (70% of Class B), about 42% of total votes but roughly 10% of the economic interest (Feb 2026 proxy). At $82.34 that stake is worth roughly $2.0B.

Plan

'Volume first': hold production near 80k+ homes a year, keep land off balance sheet, cut build costs and cycle times with technology, and wait for incentives to normalise toward 4-6%.

Pay

FY2025 total pay $29.5M for Miller, mostly stock awards.

Governance

Dual-class shares; 2026 proposals targeting the structure failed. Jaffe (co-CEO) and the COO role were not replaced, so key-person risk is concentrated.

Capital allocation, last 12 months

Buybacks: $993M cash in TTM to Aug-26 (plus 8.0M shares retired via the Millrose exchange in Q4 FY25). Diluted shares down 7.0% YoY.

Dividends: $2.00 per share a year (about $0.5B); 9M FY26 paid $366M.

Free cash flow TTM: $812M, below buybacks plus dividends of about $1.5B. The gap was funded by running cash down from $3.4B to $1.2B and adding debt.

M&A: none in FY26. Last deal Rausch Coleman (Feb 2025, $254M cash outflow for acquisitions in FY25); returns not disclosed.

Spin-offs: Millrose (Feb 2025) moved about $5B+ of land off the balance sheet; equity fell from $27.4B (Aug 2024) to $22.6B (Aug 2025).

Read: Management owns a lot and thinks long term, and has kept returning cash. But capital returns ($1.36B in 9M FY26) now exceed free cash flow, and the strategy has not yet produced the promised margin recovery. Judge them on the FY27 margin guide.

8. Risks

What specifically would break the story?

Mortgage rates stay at or above 7%. Rates rose from about 6.4% to about 7% during Q3 and recent reports cite about 7.5%. Each step up forces bigger buydowns, which come straight out of gross margin.

Margin floor fails. Q4 guide is 15.5-16.0%. If incentives cannot fall from about 12%, ROIC stays near 5-6%, below any reasonable cost of capital (roughly 9-10% for a cyclical builder).

Volume strategy turns against it. Inventory of finished homes and work in progress rose from $8.8B to $10.7B in nine months while cash fell from $3.4B to $1.2B. Unsold spec homes in a weak market mean more discounting.

Leverage creeping up. Net homebuilding debt rose to $3.1B (12.7% of capital) from $0.6B at FY25 year-end, and Lennar drew $650M on its revolver. Buybacks and dividends ($1.36B in 9M FY26) exceeded cash generation.

Demand shock. NAHB builder confidence fell to 25 in November 2026, the weakest since 2012, with 46% of builders cutting prices.

Key-person and governance. One person is chairman, CEO and president and controls about 42% of votes.

Earnings quality noise. Mark-to-market swings on technology investments ($-53M in Q3 FY26, $+99M a year earlier) blur the run rate.

Read: The story breaks if rates stay high long enough that Lennar must keep 12%+ incentives into 2027 while it carries more inventory and more debt. That combination would push ROIC further below its cost of capital.

1. Business overview

What does it do, how does it make money, and how did it get here?

Lennar is the second-largest US homebuilder by deliveries (82,583 homes in FY2025). It buys or options land, builds mostly entry-level and first move-up single-family homes (average price about $372,000 in Q3 FY2026) in roughly two dozen states, and sells them with an 'Everything's Included' feature package. It earns a second, smaller profit pool by writing the mortgage and title policy for most of its own buyers. Since 2025 it runs a 'land-light' model: it owns under 2.5% of about 488,000 homesites it controls, renting land via option contracts (largely with Millrose Properties, spun off in 2025) and paying for lots only when it is ready to build.

Read: Over 95% of revenue and essentially all of the profit come from building and selling homes. Lennar is a manufacturing-and-sales machine for starter homes, not a land speculator any more, which is the point of the 2025 Millrose spin-off.
2. Moat

Why does it earn its returns, and can competitors copy it?

Real advantages
Scale on cost: construction costs down about 12-13% over two years and cycle time at a record low (116 days in Q3 FY26 per company commentary). Volume gives buying power with trades and suppliers that small builders lack.
Land-light balance sheet: controlling about 98% of lots by option means less capital tied up in dirt and lower write-down risk, which should lift asset turns once margins normalise.
Captive mortgage and title: Financial Services earned $323M in 9M FY26 (on $679M revenue) and lets Lennar fund rate buydowns that smaller rivals cannot match.
Standardised, even-flow production ('Everything's Included', limited options) keeps the factory running at a steady pace.
What limits the moat
Homes are a near-commodity: buyers compare on price and payment, and existing-home sellers now compete directly in Lennar's price bands.
The volume-first strategy hands margin to the customer: incentives of about 12-14% of price in FY26 versus a 4-6% 'normal' level.
Peers (D.R. Horton, NVR, PulteGroup) have the same scale or the same option-land model and earn far higher margins and ROIC today.
Option land is not free: lot option fees to land bankers are a cost that sits inside gross margin.
Read: The moat is cost and scale, not pricing power. That is a real but narrow advantage: it lets Lennar survive a downturn and keep volume, but the current numbers show it does not let Lennar keep margin. Moat strength: moderate, cyclical.

Over the maximum sample, CAPM (FF Mkt−RF) α = 4.72%/yr (HAC p = 0.2914); FF3 α = 5.83%/yr (HAC p = 0.1996); Carhart 4 α = 7.09%/yr (HAC p = 0.1034); FF5 α = 5.20%/yr (HAC p = 0.2654). Rolling windows with significant alpha (either sign): 6% of 36-month and 16% of 60-month windows.

Analyst commentary

No significant alpha anywhere. None of the five CAPM windows, and none of the 20 factor-model regressions (CAPM on the FF market factor, FF3, Carhart and FF5, each over 36, 60, 120 and 180 months and the full sample), produces an intercept significant at 5% under Newey-West HAC inference. The smallest factor-model p-value is Carhart over the full sample (α = 7.09%/yr, p = 0.103).

Long-run point estimates are positive but imprecise. Over the full 415-month sample (Mar 1992 – Sep 2026) CAPM α is 4.50%/yr (×12) with a 95% HAC interval of roughly −4.5% to +13.5% per year. 120- and 180-month estimates are similar (6.5% and 5.4%/yr) with the same conclusion: the data cannot distinguish SNPS from zero alpha.

The most recent three years are sharply negative. The 36-month window (Oct 2023 – Sep 2026) shows α of −25.3%/yr (HAC t = −1.89, p = 0.068): borderline, not significant at 5%. Over that window SNPS compounded at −1.8%/yr against +22.9%/yr for the S&P 500 TR while carrying a beta of 1.44. The largest single month in the window is Sep 2025 (−18.2% vs +3.7% for the index).

The positive-alpha era is clustered. Every statistically significant positive rolling-60-month alpha ends between Apr 2019 and Jun 2024 (16% of 60-month windows); no 60-month window shows significant negative alpha. That period is now rolling out of the window, which is why the latest 60-month α is −3.3%/yr.

Beta is above one, but not decisively. Full-sample β = 1.19 (OLS test of β = 1: p = 0.054). Every window's 95% HAC beta interval includes 1. Rolling beta has moved through three regimes: about 1.5–2.9 before 2008, about 0.5–0.7 in 2010–14, and about 1.0–1.3 since 2017, with the 36-month figure rising to 1.44 most recently.

Style exposure: a persistent growth tilt. HML loadings are negative and highly significant in FF3 over 60–180 months (−0.69 to −0.72, HAC p ≤ 0.008). In FF5, part of that tilt moves into CMA (−0.61 at 180 months, p = 0.032), which is consistent with a high-investment, growth profile. Size, profitability (RMW) and momentum loadings are not significant in any window.

Idiosyncratic risk dominates. CAPM R² is only 0.25–0.37; residual volatility is 21–30% a year. At the full-sample α the implied information ratio is about 0.15, well below the level that would make a historical alpha estimate statistically robust over 34 years.

Formulas

CAPM: (R_i,t − R_f,t) = α + β·(R_m,t − R_f,t) + ε_t, OLS with intercept, t = 1…T

Returns: R_t = P_t / P_(t−1) − 1, P = last available month-end total-return level (Adj Close / TR index)

β: Cov(y,x) / Var(x) α: ȳ − β·x̄ R² = ρ²(y,x) (single regressor)

SE (OLS): σ̂²·(X'X)⁻¹, σ̂² = SSR/(T−2)

SE (HAC): Newey-West, Bartlett kernel, lag L = ⌊4·(T/100)^(2/9)⌋, small-sample factor T/(T−k);

inference uses t(T−k). Lags used:

36→3, 60→3, 120→4, 180→4, MAX(T=415)→5

Annualisation: arithmetic α_ann = 12·α (primary). (1+α)^12 − 1 is a mechanical compounding transform of the

intercept, NOT a realised investment return.

Jensen's α: mean(R_i − R_f) − β·mean(R_m − R_f) — algebraically identical to the OLS intercept on the same sample.

Geometric Jensen:(CAGR_i − CAGR_f) − β·(CAGR_m − CAGR_f); differs from 12·α by ≈ ½(σ²_i − β·σ²_m) (volatility drag) plus

compounding/cross terms.

Raw excess: CAGR_i − CAGR_m (realised, geometric) and 12·mean(R_i − R_m) (arithmetic). Not risk-adjusted.

Residual vol: √(SSR/(T−k))·√12. Total vol: sd(R_i − R_f)·√12.

DW: Σ(e_t − e_(t−1))² / Σe_t² (≈2 ⇒ no first-order autocorrelation)

Breusch-Pagan: LM = T·R² of e² on regressors, χ²(k−1)

Significance: two-sided, 5%. Rolling-chart shading uses HAC p-values.

Assumptions

Benchmark for CAPM: SP500TR.csv (column Adj Close). Must be a total-return index.

Risk-free: Ken French RF (1-month T-bill return, Ibbotson/CRSP), monthly, from the FF3 file.

Provenance: Prices retrieved 2026-11-16 from the Yahoo Finance chart API (daily adjusted close; last trading day of each month used as the month-end level; SNPS pays no dividend, splits 2:1 in Sep-1995 and Sep-2003 are adjusted). Factors from Ken French Data Library files created using the 202609 CRSP database. Every transferred file was verified against checksums computed at source.

Factor models use Ken French factors, whose market factor (Mkt−RF, CRSP value-weighted all-US) differs from the S&P 500 TR; the "CAPM (FF Mkt−RF)" bridge row isolates that benchmark effect before adding SMB/HML/RMW/CMA/Mom.

Common sample: 1992-03 – 2026-09 (415 months). All CAPM windows end at 2026-09. Factor windows end at the last month available in every factor file used.

Incomplete months are excluded; missing months are never interpolated. As-of date: 2026-11-16.

9. Investment implications

Verdict. SNPS has not demonstrated statistically significant risk-adjusted outperformance in any window or model tested. Its long-run historical record is consistent with a modestly positive alpha (point estimates about 4–7.5% a year), but it is equally consistent with zero. The last three years run against it, with a borderline-significant negative CAPM alpha. Nothing here is a forecast.

Raw outperformance is mostly beta and growth exposure. Since March 1992, SNPS compounded at 12.4% a year against 10.9% for the S&P 500 TR, a raw gap of 1.5% a year. After adjusting for a beta of about 1.2, the realised (geometric) Jensen's alpha is about −0.2% a year. The positive arithmetic intercept of 4.5% a year is offset by volatility drag of about 4.7% a year, because SNPS's total volatility is about 35%.

Underwriting a position. Treat SNPS as a high-beta, growth-tilted holding with a large stock-specific risk component, not as a source of proven alpha. Size it off the 60-month beta of 1.22 and 29% residual volatility.

Factor hedging. The negative HML and CMA loadings mean SNPS tends to lag when value and conservative-investment factors rally. That exposure should be budgeted alongside other growth and technology holdings.

Historical vs. forward-looking. All alphas here are in-sample estimates of past average risk-adjusted returns. They are not forecasts. A significant historical intercept is consistent with skill, with a persistent unpriced risk exposure, or with a sample-specific re-rating (multiple expansion), and these cannot be separated by regression alone.

Model dependence. Compare CAPM α to the FF3/Carhart/FF5 intercepts: a large drop after adding factors means part of the "outperformance" is compensation for style exposures (e.g. negative HML/value tilt, positive RMW/profitability) rather than idiosyncratic return.

Beta for risk budgeting. Use the 60-month HAC beta and its confidence interval for position sizing; the 36-month estimate is noisier, and the rolling chart shows how unstable a single point estimate can be.

Residual (idiosyncratic) volatility is the relevant input for active-risk budgeting: an information ratio ≈ α_ann / residual vol.

Expected alpha going forward should be shrunk heavily toward zero; the width of the α confidence intervals is the honest measure of how little the history pins it down.

1. Executive summary
Conclusion (historical evidence only). No CAPM window shows statistically significant positive alpha for SNPS at the 5% level using Newey-West HAC inference. The historical record does not reject zero risk-adjusted outperformance. Over the maximum sample, CAPM (FF Mkt−RF) α = 4.72%/yr (HAC p = 0.2914); FF3 α = 5.83%/yr (HAC p = 0.1996); Carhart 4 α = 7.09%/yr (HAC p = 0.1034); FF5 α = 5.20%/yr (HAC p = 0.2654). Rolling windows with significant alpha (either sign): 6% of 36-month and 16% of 60-month windows.
Analyst commentary
No significant alpha anywhere. None of the five CAPM windows, and none of the 20 factor-model regressions (CAPM on the FF market factor, FF3, Carhart and FF5, each over 36, 60, 120 and 180 months and the full sample), produces an intercept significant at 5% under Newey-West HAC inference. The smallest factor-model p-value is Carhart over the full sample (α = 7.09%/yr, p = 0.103).
Long-run point estimates are positive but imprecise. Over the full 415-month sample (Mar 1992 – Sep 2026) CAPM α is 4.50%/yr (×12) with a 95% HAC interval of roughly −4.5% to +13.5% per year. 120- and 180-month estimates are similar (6.5% and 5.4%/yr) with the same conclusion: the data cannot distinguish SNPS from zero alpha.
The most recent three years are sharply negative. The 36-month window (Oct 2023 – Sep 2026) shows α of −25.3%/yr (HAC t = −1.89, p = 0.068): borderline, not significant at 5%. Over that window SNPS compounded at −1.8%/yr against +22.9%/yr for the S&P 500 TR while carrying a beta of 1.44. The largest single month in the window is Sep 2025 (−18.2% vs +3.7% for the index).
The positive-alpha era is clustered. Every statistically significant positive rolling-60-month alpha ends between Apr 2019 and Jun 2024 (16% of 60-month windows); no 60-month window shows significant negative alpha. That period is now rolling out of the window, which is why the latest 60-month α is −3.3%/yr.
Beta is above one, but not decisively. Full-sample β = 1.19 (OLS test of β = 1: p = 0.054). Every window's 95% HAC beta interval includes 1. Rolling beta has moved through three regimes: about 1.5–2.9 before 2008, about 0.5–0.7 in 2010–14, and about 1.0–1.3 since 2017, with the 36-month figure rising to 1.44 most recently.
Style exposure: a persistent growth tilt. HML loadings are negative and highly significant in FF3 over 60–180 months (−0.69 to −0.72, HAC p ≤ 0.008). In FF5, part of that tilt moves into CMA (−0.61 at 180 months, p = 0.032), which is consistent with a high-investment, growth profile. Size, profitability (RMW) and momentum loadings are not significant in any window.
Idiosyncratic risk dominates. CAPM R² is only 0.25–0.37; residual volatility is 21–30% a year. At the full-sample α the implied information ratio is about 0.15, well below the level that would make a historical alpha estimate statistically robust over 34 years.

Formulas
CAPM:            (R_i,t − R_f,t) = α + β·(R_m,t − R_f,t) + ε_t,   OLS with intercept, t = 1…T
Returns:         R_t = P_t / P_(t−1) − 1, P = last available month-end total-return level (Adj Close / TR index)
β:               Cov(y,x) / Var(x)          α: ȳ − β·x̄          R² = ρ²(y,x) (single regressor)
SE (OLS):        σ̂²·(X'X)⁻¹, σ̂² = SSR/(T−2)
SE (HAC):        Newey-West, Bartlett kernel, lag L = ⌊4·(T/100)^(2/9)⌋, small-sample factor T/(T−k);
                 inference uses t(T−k). Lags used: 
                 36→3, 60→3, 120→4, 180→4, MAX(T=415)→5
Annualisation:   arithmetic α_ann = 12·α (primary).  (1+α)^12 − 1 is a mechanical compounding transform of the
                 intercept, NOT a realised investment return.
Jensen's α:      mean(R_i − R_f) − β·mean(R_m − R_f)  — algebraically identical to the OLS intercept on the same sample.
Geometric Jensen:(CAGR_i − CAGR_f) − β·(CAGR_m − CAGR_f); differs from 12·α by ≈ ½(σ²_i − β·σ²_m) (volatility drag) plus
                 compounding/cross terms.
Raw excess:      CAGR_i − CAGR_m (realised, geometric) and 12·mean(R_i − R_m) (arithmetic). Not risk-adjusted.
Residual vol:    √(SSR/(T−k))·√12.   Total vol: sd(R_i − R_f)·√12.
DW:              Σ(e_t − e_(t−1))² / Σe_t²  (≈2 ⇒ no first-order autocorrelation)
Breusch-Pagan:   LM = T·R² of e² on regressors, χ²(k−1)
Significance:    two-sided, 5%. Rolling-chart shading uses HAC p-values.

Benchmark for CAPM: SP500TR.csv (column Adj Close). Must be a total-return index.
Risk-free: Ken French RF (1-month T-bill return, Ibbotson/CRSP), monthly, from the FF3 file.
Provenance: Prices retrieved 2026-11-16 from the Yahoo Finance chart API (daily adjusted close; last trading day of each month used as the month-end level; SNPS pays no dividend, splits 2:1 in Sep-1995 and Sep-2003 are adjusted). Factors from Ken French Data Library files created using the 202609 CRSP database. Every transferred file was verified against checksums computed at source.
Factor models use Ken French factors, whose market factor (Mkt−RF, CRSP value-weighted all-US) differs from the S&P 500 TR; the "CAPM (FF Mkt−RF)" bridge row isolates that benchmark effect before adding SMB/HML/RMW/CMA/Mom.

9. Investment implications
Verdict. SNPS has not demonstrated statistically significant risk-adjusted outperformance in any window or model tested. Its long-run historical record is consistent with a modestly positive alpha (point estimates about 4–7.5% a year), but it is equally consistent with zero. The last three years run against it, with a borderline-significant negative CAPM alpha. Nothing here is a forecast.
Raw outperformance is mostly beta and growth exposure. Since March 1992, SNPS compounded at 12.4% a year against 10.9% for the S&P 500 TR, a raw gap of 1.5% a year. After adjusting for a beta of about 1.2, the realised (geometric) Jensen's alpha is about −0.2% a year. The positive arithmetic intercept of 4.5% a year is offset by volatility drag of about 4.7% a year, because SNPS's total volatility is about 35%.
Underwriting a position. Treat SNPS as a high-beta, growth-tilted holding with a large stock-specific risk component, not as a source of proven alpha. Size it off the 60-month beta of 1.22 and 29% residual volatility.
Factor hedging. The negative HML and CMA loadings mean SNPS tends to lag when value and conservative-investment factors rally. That exposure should be budgeted alongside other growth and technology holdings.
Historical vs. forward-looking. All alphas here are in-sample estimates of past average risk-adjusted returns. They are not forecasts. A significant historical intercept is consistent with skill, with a persistent unpriced risk exposure, or with a sample-specific re-rating (multiple expansion), and these cannot be separated by regression alone.
Model dependence. Compare CAPM α to the FF3/Carhart/FF5 intercepts: a large drop after adding factors means part of the "outperformance" is compensation for style exposures (e.g. negative HML/value tilt, positive RMW/profitability) rather than idiosyncratic return.
Beta for risk budgeting. Use the 60-month HAC beta and its confidence interval for position sizing; the 36-month estimate is noisier, and the rolling chart shows how unstable a single point estimate can be.
Residual (idiosyncratic) volatility is the relevant input for active-risk budgeting: an information ratio ≈ α_ann / residual vol.
Expected alpha going forward should be shrunk heavily toward zero; the width of the α confidence intervals is the honest measure of how little the history pins it down.

What does it do, how does it make money, and how did it get here?

What it does

Underwriting (~70% of revenue): ISO policy forms, rules and loss costs; AIR catastrophe models; property data and aerial imagery; specialty and life insurance software.

Claims (~30%): Xactimate repair estimating for adjusters and contractors; ClaimSearch anti-fraud database; casualty and digital media forensics tools.

Subscriptions (84% of revenue): multi-year, annually escalating licences for data, models and software.

Transactional (16%): per-use fees that rise and fall with claims volume, storms and policy activity.

1. Business overview

What does it do, how does it make money, and how did it get here?

What it does. SK hynix designs and manufactures memory chips: DRAM (working memory, about 75% of Q3 2026 revenue, roughly 78T won) and NAND flash (storage, roughly 25T won, including enterprise SSDs from its Solidigm unit). Its crown jewel is HBM (high-bandwidth memory), stacked DRAM that sits next to AI accelerators such as Nvidia's GPUs.

How it makes money. It sells chips by the bit. Profit is driven by price per bit minus cost per bit; cost falls as it moves to denser process nodes (1c DRAM, 321-layer NAND). Fabs are mostly in Korea (Icheon, Cheongju M15X, Yongin under construction), with DRAM and NAND fabs in China.

Who buys. AI accelerator makers and cloud providers. Long-term agreements (LTAs) with 14 customers cover more than half of 2027-2028 capacity, typically for about five years, with prices moving inside an agreed band.

1994 Today's CEO joins Hyundai Electronics' chip R&D, the company's predecessor

2012 SK Group takes control; becomes SK hynix

2022 Kwak Noh-jung becomes co-CEO (sole CEO from late 2023)

2023 Memory bust: operating margin about -24%

2025 Record year: 97.1T won revenue, 47.2T op. profit, beats Samsung's total op. profit

Jul 2026 $26.5B Nasdaq ADR listing, largest ever by a foreign company; Kioxia stake partly sold (Q2 gain)

Oct 2026 First quarter above 100T won revenue; ~100T won FY26 shareholder-return plan

Read: A near pure-play memory maker that turned from a 2023 loss into the world's most profitable memory company on the back of AI. That means earnings are tied to the memory price cycle, not to a product with sticky pricing.

2. Moat

Why does it earn its returns, and can competitors copy it?

Real advantages (USPs)

HBM leadership: #1 HBM supplier by revenue (50% in Q2 2026, Counterpoint); reportedly over two-thirds of HBM4 volume for Nvidia's Vera Rubin.

Process and packaging know-how: HBM4 in full mass production in Q3 2026; 1c DRAM and 321-layer NAND ramping. Yield on stacked dies is hard to copy quickly.

Customer qualification: getting designed into an accelerator takes many months; LTAs with 14 customers lock in volume through 2028.

Scale and balance sheet: 98.7T won net cash funds capex through a downturn without borrowing.

Why it is not a wide moat

DRAM and NAND are standardized commodities; three players (plus CXMT) can make substitutes.

HBM share already slipping: 64% (Q2 2025) to 50% (Q2 2026) as Samsung reached 33%.

Returns attract capacity: SK hynix, Samsung, Micron and CXMT are all expanding; new fabs arrive in 3-5 years.

Morningstar rates SK hynix as having no economic moat and 'very high' uncertainty.

Read: The edge is a technology and timing lead in HBM, not a structural moat. It earns 80% margins today because supply is short; the lead is real but must be re-won every product generation (HBM3E, HBM4, HBM4E).

Read: At roughly 2.5x next year's earnings in Seoul (3.7x on the ADR) the market is pricing a sharp earnings fall, not a continuation. That is cheap against its own 9.2x long-run average and in line with Micron and Samsung, which are priced the same way. The ADR costs about 45% more than the same claim on Seoul shares; anyone who can buy 000660 directly gets the same business for less. PEG is near zero and not meaningful at a cycle peak.

6. Industry and competitors

How fast is the market growing, and how does SK hynix stack up on fundamentals and price?

DRAM market revenue grew 57% QoQ and 385% YoY in Q2 2026 (Counterpoint).

SK hynix expects 2027 bit demand growth of mid-20s % for DRAM and high-teens % for NAND, and demand above supply through 2030.

Cloud providers are expected to lift capex by more than 60% next year; data-center memory estimated at $237B in 2026 (SemiAnalysis).

Supply response: all three majors plan large capex increases for 2027; CXMT's DRAM share rose from 4% to 10% in a year.

Company Price (date) Market cap Operating margin HBM share Q2'26 DRAM share Q2'26 P/E TTM Fwd P/E EV/EBITDA Net cash

Read: SK hynix has the best margin and HBM position of the group but the smallest DRAM share; the market prices all three memory makers at 3-4x forward earnings, so there is no SK hynix-specific discount in Seoul. Peer multiples mix fiscal years (Micron FY ends August) and Samsung's forward P/E is derived from a broker's implied multiple; treat them as rough.

7. Management and capital allocation

Who runs it, what do they own, and what do they do with the cash?

CEO Kwak Noh-jung: joined the predecessor in 1994 as a researcher, CEO since March 2022 (sole CEO since late 2023), retained in SK Group's Oct 2026 reshuffle.

Ownership: CEO holds about 0.002% of shares. SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won bought his first 3,620 shares in July 2026.

Controlling holder: SK Square owns about 20%, rising as bought-back shares are cancelled. In Sept 2026 SK Group placed three vice chairpersons in strategic roles at SK hynix.

Plan: maximize M15X, raise 1c DRAM share, ramp Yongin Phase 1 in 2027, make HBM4 the mainstream product, build a $10B US AI-solutions unit.

Policy: return at least 50% of free cash flow.

FY2026: about 100T won of returns: ≥30T dividends (Q3 alone 14T won, 20,000 won/share incl. a 10,000 won Kioxia special) and ≥60T buybacks/cancellations.

Capex: high-40T won in 2026 (about 15% of revenue); 2027 to rise 'significantly'.

Balance sheet: net cash went from 3.8T (Sep-25) to 98.7T won (Sep-26).

Watch: 10T won of buyback shares go to employee compensation, a real cost not visible in SBC.

Read: A career engineer CEO with negligible ownership, under a controlling group. Capital allocation in this upcycle has been shareholder-friendly (big cancellations, high payout) while keeping a large cash buffer for the next downturn. The key test is 2027 capex discipline.

8. Risks

What would break the story?

Risk What it looks like Signal to watch

Memory price cycle Operating margin went 52% (2018) to 10% (2019) and -24% (2023). Q3 2026 profit came mostly from price. DRAM contract prices; Micron's Dec margin guide

Supply response All majors raise 2027 capex; Yongin, Samsung HBM4, Micron, CXMT capacity. Capex guides in Jan 2027; inventory days (118 in Q3)

HBM share loss Share fell from 64% to 50% in a year; brokers (LS) cut 2027 HBM margin assumption from ~80% to ~60%. Nvidia Vera Rubin supplier split; HBM4 pricing

Customer and AI-spend concentration Nvidia and hyperscalers dominate HBM demand; Nov 2026 sell-off on US midterm results and data-center limits; Nvidia leadership uncertainty. Hyperscaler capex guidance; US data-center rules

China exposure 24.3% of Q1 2026 sales from China; China fabs need annual US equipment approval. US export-control decisions

ADR premium collapse SKHY trades ~45% above Seoul value because new ADR creation is restricted. If conversion opens, ADR holders could lose that premium even if the business does fine. ADR premium; depositary/conversion rule changes

Non-operating volatility 22.9T won investment-asset loss and 11.6T won FX loss in Q3; asset not named. Q4 non-operating line

Currency Revenue in USD, reporting in KRW; ADR holders also carry KRW/USD. KRW/USD

9. Scenarios (12 months, per SKHY ADR)

Bear / base / bull, with analyst consensus as the reference point. Scenario values are my estimates.

Bear

$75

-43% vs $131.79

DRAM prices roll over in H2 2027 as new capacity lands; 2027 EPS ~40% below consensus (~$21/ADR)

HBM margins compress toward 60% as Samsung takes share

ADR premium narrows from ~45% to ~15%; 3.5x P/E on falling earnings

Base

$159

21% vs $131.79

2027 EPS in line with consensus ($35.34/ADR)

Prices plateau, volume growth mid-20s %; LTAs hold

Multiple stays near the 4.0-4.5x seen since listing; premium persists

Bull

$245

86% vs $131.79

2027 EPS 15% above consensus (~$40.6, back to July estimate) on HBM4 pricing

Shortage persists through 2028 as the company guides

Re-rating to ~6x as investors stop pricing a bust

Where consensus sits: the average target of ~$243 (range $200-$400; Rosenblatt high at $400 ≈ 9x NTM earnings) is close to my bull case, because it assumes the multiple re-rates. Morningstar's fair value is $160, near the base case. Consensus 2027 EPS has already been cut from $40.47 to $35.34 in three months.

10. Takeaways

Remember

A superb business right now: 80% operating margin, ROIC above 100%, 98.7T won net cash.

Not a wide moat: an HBM lead in a commodity industry, and the lead is narrowing.

The stock prices a bust: ~2.5x forward earnings in Seoul, ~3.7x on the ADR, vs a 9.2x long-run average.

The ADR carries a ~45% premium to Seoul shares; that is a separate, avoidable risk.

Net profit is noisy (Kioxia gain, investment and FX losses); use operating profit and FCF.

Check next

Q4 2026 results on 28 Jan 2027: did DRAM bits grow mid-20s %? What is the 2027 capex number?

DRAM and HBM contract price trends into 2027; Micron's Dec 2026 results.

HBM4 share at Nvidia Rubin vs Samsung.

Name of the asset behind the 22.9T won investment loss.

ADR premium and any change to ADR conversion rules.

Full quarterly report (cash flow and balance sheet) to firm up TTM FCF and ROIC.

Glossary

HBM

High-bandwidth memory: DRAM dies stacked vertically and placed next to an AI chip.

ASP

Average selling price, here per bit of memory.

Bit growth

Growth in total memory capacity shipped.

LTA

Long-term supply agreement with a customer.

ADR

American depositary receipt; 10 SKHY ADRs = 1 Seoul share.

NOPAT

Operating profit after tax, before financing items.

ROIC

NOPAT / invested capital: how much profit each won tied up in the business earns.

FCF conversion

FCF / NOPAT: how much accounting profit turns into cash.

PEG

P/E divided by expected EPS growth (in %).

7. Management and capital allocation

Who runs it, what do they own, and what do they do with the cash?

CEO Kwak Noh-jung: joined the predecessor in 1994 as a researcher, CEO since March 2022 (sole CEO since late 2023), retained in SK Group's Oct 2026 reshuffle.
Ownership: CEO holds about 0.002% of shares. SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won bought his first 3,620 shares in July 2026.
Controlling holder: SK Square owns about 20%, rising as bought-back shares are cancelled. In Sept 2026 SK Group placed three vice chairpersons in strategic roles at SK hynix.
Plan: maximize M15X, raise 1c DRAM share, ramp Yongin Phase 1 in 2027, make HBM4 the mainstream product, build a $10B US AI-solutions unit.
Policy: return at least 50% of free cash flow.
FY2026: about 100T won of returns: ≥30T dividends (Q3 alone 14T won, 20,000 won/share incl. a 10,000 won Kioxia special) and ≥60T buybacks/cancellations.

Read: A career engineer CEO with negligible ownership, under a controlling group. Capital allocation in this upcycle has been shareholder-friendly (big cancellations, high payout) while keeping a large cash buffer for the next downturn. The key test is 2027 capex discipline.

Where consensus sits: the average target of ~$243 (range $200-$400; Rosenblatt high at $400 ≈ 9x NTM earnings) is close to my bull case, because it assumes the multiple re-rates. Morningstar's fair value is $160, near the base case. Consensus 2027 EPS has already been cut from $40.47 to $35.34 in three months.
10. Takeaways
Remember
A superb business right now: 80% operating margin, ROIC above 100%, 98.7T won net cash.
Not a wide moat: an HBM lead in a commodity industry, and the lead is narrowing.
The stock prices a bust: ~2.5x forward earnings in Seoul, ~3.7x on the ADR, vs a 9.2x long-run average.
The ADR carries a ~45% premium to Seoul shares; that is a separate, avoidable risk.
Net profit is noisy (Kioxia gain, investment and FX losses); use operating profit and FCF.

High-bandwidth memory: DRAM dies stacked vertically and placed next to an AI chip.
ASP

ADR

NOPAT

ROIC

1. Business overview

What does it do, how does it make money, how did it get here?

Synopsys sells the software, hardware and pre-built circuit blocks that engineers use to design and verify chips, and (since buying Ansys in July 2025) the simulation software used to test physical systems such as engines, antennas and batteries. Almost every advanced chip passes through Synopsys or Cadence tools before it is manufactured. Customers are chip designers (Nvidia, AMD, Apple, Qualcomm, hyperscalers) and foundries; contracts are mostly multi-year licences, so 82% of revenue is recurring.

How it makes money (TTM to Jul-2026)

Design Automation (EDA software + hardware + Ansys simulation)

$7,674m · 81%

Design IP (interface, memory, logic libraries, security IP)

$1,742m · 19%

Timeline

1986Founded by Aart de Geus and colleagues out of GE's microelectronics centre; its logic-synthesis tool (Design Compiler) becomes the industry standard.

1992IPO on Nasdaq.

2000s-2010sRoll-up of the design flow: Avant! (place & route), Magma, Synplicity and many IP firms. Builds the #1 interface-IP business.

Jan 2024Sassine Ghazi becomes CEO; de Geus moves to executive chair.

Sep 2024Sells the Software Integrity (app security) unit to focus on silicon-to-systems.

Jul 2025Closes the ~$35bn Ansys acquisition; debt rises to ~$14bn.

Sep 2025Q3 FY25 miss driven by Design IP; stock falls 22% after hours.

Dec 2025Nvidia invests $2bn in Synopsys; FY25 revenue $7.05bn, backlog $11.4bn.

May 2026Settlement with activist Elliott; Jesse Cohn joins the board.

Sep 2026Investor Day: FY27 guide $11.15bn revenue, ~44% margin, ~50% margin by FY30, ~$1bn buyback intent, $1bn+ Amazon IP deal, OpenAI partnership.

Read: a toll-road business that just doubled its toll booths. Core EDA is a near-monopoly-like duopoly; Ansys adds about $2.9bn of simulation revenue a year. The price was a $26.8bn goodwill balance and $10bn of debt, so the next three years are about proving the deal earns its cost.

2. Moat and USPs

Why does it earn its returns, and can competitors copy it?

Source Why it matters Strength

Switching costs Design flows, scripts and sign-off methods are built around one vendor's tools; a tool switch mid-project risks a failed tape-out costing $100m+. Very strong

Foundry co-optimization Tools are certified with TSMC, Samsung and Intel at each new node (2nm and below). A newcomer must re-earn this every node. Very strong

Duopoly scale Synopsys and Cadence together design virtually every chip; Siemens EDA is a distant third. R&D of ~$2.8bn/yr is hard to match. Strong

IP library ('build once, sell many') #1 in interface IP (PCIe, DDR/LPDDR, die-to-die). Each block is reused across hundreds of chips at near-zero marginal cost. Strong, but execution slipped in FY25

Ansys physics solvers Decades-old, validated multiphysics solvers (fluids, structures, electromagnetics) used for certification in aerospace and autos. Strong

Data and AI Proprietary design data and solvers feed AI agents (AgentEngineer, Autopilot). Rivals face the same option, so this is a race, not a moat yet. Unproven

Read: the moat is real and mostly about switching costs and foundry certification, not brand. What is less secure is pricing power in Design IP (segment margin fell from ~38% in FY24 to 16% in Q1 FY26 before recovering to 26.5% in Q3) and whether AI lets customers or Cadence capture more of the value.

3. Revenue drivers

Volume x price x mix, and the KPIs that move it

Revenue = design activity (number and complexity of chip and system projects) x licences and seats per project x price per licence + IP blocks licensed (and, increasingly, royalties per unit shipped) + simulation seats (Ansys). AI raises all three: more custom chips, bigger designs (multi-die, 3D packaging), and AI agents that consume more licence-hours.

KPI Latest Why it matters

EDA growth (organic) +8.5% YoY in Q3 FY26 Guided to double digits in Q4 and FY26. The core of valuation.

Design IP revenue $474m, +11% YoY, 2nd straight quarter of growth Long-term floor now 17% CAGR; watch margins (26.5%).

Ansys / Simulation & Analysis revenue $711m in Q3; ~$2.98bn FY26 guide Floor 10% CAGR; $400m revenue synergies by FY29.

Backlog $10.9bn (down from $11.4bn at FY25 end, mainly divested Processor IP) ~1.1x annual revenue: high visibility.

Non-GAAP operating margin 41.6% in Q3; 41.5% FY26 guide Target ~44% FY27, ~50% FY30.

China share of revenue ~10% in Q2 FY26 (14% in Q3 FY25) Export-control sensitivity.

Read: headline growth of 42% is mostly Ansys arriving. Strip that out and the old Synopsys grew roughly 6-9% in Q3 (divestitures muddy the base). The story the market is underwriting is that core EDA re-accelerates to low teens and IP returns to high teens.

The discount reflects lower GAAP returns after Ansys, IP execution scars and leverage. On GAAP numbers it looks expensive (~82x), which is mostly amortization noise.

6. Industry and competitors

Growth prospects and peers on fundamentals and valuation

EDA is a roughly $20bn+ niche growing faster than software as a whole, driven by AI accelerators, custom silicon at hyperscalers, chiplets and 3D packaging, and more simulation in cars and aerospace. 1. Business overview
What does it do, how does it make money, how did it get here?

Synopsys sells the software, hardware and pre-built circuit blocks that engineers use to design and verify chips, and (since buying Ansys in July 2025) the simulation software used to test physical systems such as engines, antennas and batteries. Almost every advanced chip passes through Synopsys or Cadence tools before it is manufactured. Customers are chip designers (Nvidia, AMD, Apple, Qualcomm, hyperscalers) and foundries; contracts are mostly multi-year licences, so 82% of revenue is recurring.

2. Moat and USPs
Why does it earn its returns, and can competitors copy it?
Source	Why it matters	Strength
Switching costs	Design flows, scripts and sign-off methods are built around one vendor's tools; a tool switch mid-project risks a failed tape-out costing $100m+.	Very strong
Foundry co-optimization	Tools are certified with TSMC, Samsung and Intel at each new node (2nm and below). A newcomer must re-earn this every node.	Very strong
Duopoly scale	Synopsys and Cadence together design virtually every chip; Siemens EDA is a distant third. R&D of ~$2.8bn/yr is hard to match.	Strong
IP library ('build once, sell many')	#1 in interface IP (PCIe, DDR/LPDDR, die-to-die). Each block is reused across hundreds of chips at near-zero marginal cost.	Strong, but execution slipped in FY25
Ansys physics solvers	Decades-old, validated multiphysics solvers (fluids, structures, electromagnetics) used for certification in aerospace and autos.	Strong
Data and AI	Proprietary design data and solvers feed AI agents (AgentEngineer, Autopilot). Rivals face the same option, so this is a race, not a moat yet.	Unproven
Read: the moat is real and mostly about switching costs and foundry certification, not brand. What is less secure is pricing power in Design IP (segment margin fell from ~38% in FY24 to 16% in Q1 FY26 before recovering to 26.5% in Q3) and whether AI lets customers or Cadence capture more of the value.

Revenue = design activity (number and complexity of chip and system projects) x licences and seats per project x price per licence + IP blocks licensed (and, increasingly, royalties per unit shipped) + simulation seats (Ansys). AI raises all three: more custom chips, bigger designs (multi-die, 3D packaging), and AI agents that consume more licence-hours.

1. Business overview

What does it do, how does it make money, and how did it get here?

What it does. Lam designs, builds and services the machines that etch (carve) and deposit (lay down) the ultra-thin material layers that make up a chip. Every memory chip (DRAM, NAND, HBM) and every advanced logic chip passes through Lam tools hundreds of times. It does not make chips; it sells the "picks and shovels" to the people who do.

How it makes money. Two streams. Systems (64% of FY2026 revenue): one-off sales of new tools, each costing millions of dollars, driven by customers' fab spending. Customer Support (CSBG) (36%): spare parts, service contracts, upgrades and refurbished legacy tools sold into an installed base that keeps running for decades. Systems is cyclical; CSBG is steadier and grows with the installed base.

Who pays. A concentrated club: Micron, Samsung, SK hynix and TSMC were the largest customers in each of the last three years. Memory was 46% of systems revenue in the Sep-26 quarter, foundry 46%, logic and other 8%.

History and timeline

1980

Founded by David K. Lam in Fremont, California; plasma etch is the founding product.

1984

Read: A focused, two-engine model: cyclical tool sales on top of a recurring service base that is now over a third of revenue. Customer concentration and 34% China exposure are the structural features to keep in mind.

2. Moat

Why does it earn its returns, and can competitors copy it?

Process know-how and tool-of-record status. Once a fab qualifies a Lam chamber for a specific etch or deposition step, switching suppliers means re-qualifying the process, risking yield on billion-dollar lines. Customers rarely do it mid-node. Lam holds roughly 40-50% of plasma etch per industry estimates.

Leadership where complexity is rising. High-aspect-ratio etch for 3D NAND and DRAM, atomic-layer deposition and etch, molybdenum metallisation and advanced-packaging steps. Each new generation (more NAND layers, HBM stacks, gate-all-around transistors) needs more etch and deposition steps per wafer, so Lam's served market grows faster than chip output.

Installed base annuity. Decades of tools in the field feed CSBG: $8.3bn of FY2026 revenue from spares, service and upgrades, with three consecutive record quarters in 2026.

Scale in R&D. $2.4bn of R&D in FY2026 (10% of revenue), co-developed with the four largest chipmakers. Smaller or Chinese entrants can copy older steps but not the leading edge on the same timeline.

Oligopoly structure. Wafer fab equipment is effectively five large players (ASML, Applied, Lam, Tokyo Electron, KLA), each strongest in different steps. Competition is real in deposition (Applied) and etch (TEL), but pricing is disciplined.

Read: Returns are earned by switching costs plus technical leadership in the steps whose intensity rises every node. The moat is strongest in memory etch and weakest in mature-node China tools, where local suppliers are gaining.

3. Revenue drivers

What is revenue made of (volume x price x mix), and which KPIs move it?

Revenue = WFE spend x Lam's share of that spend + installed base x service per tool.

Volume: industry wafer fab equipment (WFE) spending. KLA puts calendar 2026 in the low-$150bn range; Lam's early view is above $200bn for 2027, led by DRAM, leading-edge foundry and NAND.

Price and mix: etch/deposition intensity per wafer (more steps per node), memory vs foundry mix, and leading-edge vs mature-node tools. Memory upgrades (NAND layer conversions) are high-margin.

Service: CSBG grows with tool count and fab utilisation; upgrades spike when memory makers convert existing lines.

7. Industry and competitors

How fast is the market growing, and how does Lam stack up?

Wafer fab equipment is a ~$150bn (2026) market expected to exceed $200bn in 2027 per Lam's preliminary view, driven by AI data-centre chips, high-bandwidth memory, and advanced packaging. ASML says its planned 2027-28 supply will not fully meet demand. Lam, KLA and ASML gained share in 2025 while Applied and TEL lost share (Information Network data). Strategy: ride etch/deposition intensity in AI-era memory, gate-all-around logic and advanced packaging; expand capacity (US labs, global manufacturing; ~1,900 headcount added); grow CSBG and upgrades.

Capital allocation: fund R&D first, then return ~all FCF via buybacks and a growing dividend ($0.33/quarter from Nov 2026, up from $0.26). Large M&A is rare (Novellus 2012; KLA attempt 2016).

Ownership: insiders own well under 1%; pay is ~95% equity. Insiders sold ~$176m of stock over the past 12 months (normal for equity-paid executives, but no buying).

Read: A long-tenured, internally promoted team with a shareholder-friendly, disciplined capital-return record through both up and down cycles. Skin in the game is modest in percentage terms but large in dollars.

9. Risks

The specific things that would break the story.

Cyclical downturn in WFE. Equipment is the most volatile part of the chip chain. FY2024 revenue fell 14.5%; earlier cycles were deeper. If AI or memory capex is digested in 2027-28, earnings could fall 30%+ while the multiple also compresses.

China and export controls. China was 34% of FY2026 revenue and swings sharply (26% to 35% in one quarter). New US rules, entity listings, or Chinese self-sufficiency could cut this quickly. Management already guides China 'significantly lower' in the Dec-26 quarter.

Customer concentration. Four customers (Micron, Samsung, SK hynix, TSMC) dominate. One deferring a fab ramp moves Lam's quarter.

Supply chain and execution. Component shortages and clean-room limits are already capping shipments; tariffs on aluminium and steel weighed on gross margin in FY2026.

Policy and AI-sentiment shocks. November 2026 midterm results raised fears of AI regulation and slower data-centre build-outs; the stock fell ~34% in a month with no change in Lam's own numbers.

Technology shifts. A process change that reduces etch steps (or favours a competitor's deposition approach) could erode share at a node transition.

11. Takeaways

What to remember, and what to check next.

Remember

High-quality cyclical: 35-40% operating margins, ~50-70% ROIC, net cash, ~97% of FCF returned.

Record numbers now: Sep-26 Q revenue $8.2bn (+54% y/y), Dec-26 Q guide $8.6bn.

Valuation reset: ~23x FY2027E and ~18x FY2028E EPS, below its 5-year average forward P/E.

Consensus target $363 needs both the earnings and a higher multiple.

Main risk is the cycle (WFE in 2027-28), then China.

Check next

Memory capex plans of Samsung, SK hynix, Micron for 2027.

Any new US export rules on China tools.

FCF conversion back above 90% as receivables unwind.

Glossary

WFE

Wafer fab equipment: the machines used to process silicon wafers into chips; the market Lam sells into.

Etch / deposition

Deposition lays down a thin layer of material; etch removes it in a precise pattern. Repeated hundreds of times per chip.

CSBG

Customer Support Business Group: Lam's spares, service, upgrades and refurbished-tool business.

FCF conversion

Free cash flow / net profit. Above ~90% means profits turn into cash.

ROIC

Return on invested capital: after-tax operating profit / (equity + debt - cash).

DuPont ROE

Net margin x asset turnover x equity multiplier (assets / equity).

PEG

Forward P/E divided by expected EPS growth (%). Below 1 looks cheap, but misleads at cyclical peaks.

EV/EBITDA

Enterprise value (market cap + debt - cash) / EBITDA (operating profit + depreciation and amortisation).

1. Business overview
What does it do, how does it make money, and how did it get here?

What it does. Lam designs, builds and services the machines that etch (carve) and deposit (lay down) the ultra-thin material layers that make up a chip. Every memory chip (DRAM, NAND, HBM) and every advanced logic chip passes through Lam tools hundreds of times. It does not make chips; it sells the "picks and shovels" to the people who do.

How it makes money. Two streams. Systems (64% of FY2026 revenue): one-off sales of new tools, each costing millions of dollars, driven by customers' fab spending. Customer Support (CSBG) (36%): spare parts, service contracts, upgrades and refurbished legacy tools sold into an installed base that keeps running for decades. Systems is cyclical; CSBG is steadier and grows with the installed base.

Who pays. A concentrated club: Micron, Samsung, SK hynix and TSMC were the largest customers in each of the last three years. Memory was 46% of systems revenue in the Sep-26 quarter, foundry 46%, logic and other 8%.

Read: A focused, two-engine model: cyclical tool sales on top of a recurring service base that is now over a third of revenue. Customer concentration and 34% China exposure are the structural features to keep in mind.
2. Moat
Why does it earn its returns, and can competitors copy it?
Process know-how and tool-of-record status. Once a fab qualifies a Lam chamber for a specific etch or deposition step, switching suppliers means re-qualifying the process, risking yield on billion-dollar lines. Customers rarely do it mid-node. Lam holds roughly 40-50% of plasma etch per industry estimates.
Leadership where complexity is rising. High-aspect-ratio etch for 3D NAND and DRAM, atomic-layer deposition and etch, molybdenum metallisation and advanced-packaging steps. Each new generation (more NAND layers, HBM stacks, gate-all-around transistors) needs more etch and deposition steps per wafer, so Lam's served market grows faster than chip output.
Installed base annuity. Decades of tools in the field feed CSBG: $8.3bn of FY2026 revenue from spares, service and upgrades, with three consecutive record quarters in 2026.
Scale in R&D. $2.4bn of R&D in FY2026 (10% of revenue), co-developed with the four largest chipmakers. Smaller or Chinese entrants can copy older steps but not the leading edge on the same timeline.
Oligopoly structure. Wafer fab equipment is effectively five large players (ASML, Applied, Lam, Tokyo Electron, KLA), each strongest in different steps. Competition is real in deposition (Applied) and etch (TEL), but pricing is disciplined.
Read: Returns are earned by switching costs plus technical leadership in the steps whose intensity rises every node. The moat is strongest in memory etch and weakest in mature-node China tools, where local suppliers are gaining.
3. Revenue drivers
What is revenue made of (volume x price x mix), and which KPIs move it?

Revenue = WFE spend x Lam's share of that spend + installed base x service per tool.

Volume: industry wafer fab equipment (WFE) spending. KLA puts calendar 2026 in the low-$150bn range; Lam's early view is above $200bn for 2027, led by DRAM, leading-edge foundry and NAND.
Price and mix: etch/deposition intensity per wafer (more steps per node), memory vs foundry mix, and leading-edge vs mature-node tools. Memory upgrades (NAND layer conversions) are high-margin.
Service: CSBG grows with tool count and fab utilisation; upgrades spike when memory makers convert existing lines.

7. Industry and competitors
How fast is the market growing, and how does Lam stack up?

Wafer fab equipment is a ~$150bn (2026) market expected to exceed $200bn in 2027 per Lam's preliminary view, driven by AI data-centre chips, high-bandwidth memory, and advanced packaging. ASML says its planned 2027-28 supply will not fully meet demand. Lam, KLA and ASML gained share in 2025 while Applied and TEL lost share (Information Network data). Chinese domestic toolmakers (e.g. Naura) are growing fast at mature nodes.

Read: Lam is growing faster than every large peer in the latest quarter and has the highest China exposure. The market prices all five at similar 21-29x forward multiples; the debate is the length of the cycle, not Lam's position within it.
8. Management
Who runs it, how long, what they plan, what they own, and how they allocate capital.
NAME	ROLE	TENURE	OWNERSHIP	PAY
Tim Archer	President & CEO	CEO since Dec 2018; at Lam since 2012 (ex-Novellus COO)	~0.08%	$28.3m (FY25 total comp)

Strategy: ride etch/deposition intensity in AI-era memory, gate-all-around logic and advanced packaging; expand capacity (US labs, global manufacturing; ~1,900 headcount added); grow CSBG and upgrades.
Capital allocation: fund R&D first, then return ~all FCF via buybacks and a growing dividend ($0.33/quarter from Nov 2026, up from $0.26). Large M&A is rare (Novellus 2012; KLA attempt 2016).
Ownership: insiders own well under 1%; pay is ~95% equity. Insiders sold ~$176m of stock over the past 12 months (normal for equity-paid executives, but no buying).
Read: A long-tenured, internally promoted team with a shareholder-friendly, disciplined capital-return record through both up and down cycles. Skin in the game is modest in percentage terms but large in dollars.
9. Risks
The specific things that would break the story.
Cyclical downturn in WFE. Equipment is the most volatile part of the chip chain. FY2024 revenue fell 14.5%; earlier cycles were deeper. If AI or memory capex is digested in 2027-28, earnings could fall 30%+ while the multiple also compresses.
China and export controls. China was 34% of FY2026 revenue and swings sharply (26% to 35% in one quarter). New US rules, entity listings, or Chinese self-sufficiency could cut this quickly. Management already guides China 'significantly lower' in the Dec-26 quarter.
Customer concentration. Four customers (Micron, Samsung, SK hynix, TSMC) dominate. One deferring a fab ramp moves Lam's quarter.
Supply chain and execution. Component shortages and clean-room limits are already capping shipments; tariffs on aluminium and steel weighed on gross margin in FY2026.
Policy and AI-sentiment shocks. November 2026 midterm results raised fears of AI regulation and slower data-centre build-outs; the stock fell ~34% in a month with no change in Lam's own numbers.
Technology shifts. A process change that reduces etch steps (or favours a competitor's deposition approach) could erode share at a node transition.

Read: The analyst consensus target of $363 (34 analysts) implies ~30x FY2028 consensus EPS, so it sits near the bull case, not the base case: the Street is assuming the multiple recovers as well as the earnings arriving. The asymmetry hinges almost entirely on whether 2027-28 WFE holds.
11. Takeaways
What to remember, and what to check next.
Remember
High-quality cyclical: 35-40% operating margins, ~50-70% ROIC, net cash, ~97% of FCF returned.
Record numbers now: Sep-26 Q revenue $8.2bn (+54% y/y), Dec-26 Q guide $8.6bn.
Valuation reset: ~23x FY2027E and ~18x FY2028E EPS, below its 5-year average forward P/E.
Consensus target $363 needs both the earnings and a higher multiple.
Main risk is the cycle (WFE in 2027-28), then China.
Check next
Dec-26 quarter (late Jan 2027): revenue vs $8.6bn guide, China share, deferred revenue.
First firm 2027 WFE outlook from Lam, ASML (27 Jan) and Applied (12 Nov).
Memory capex plans of Samsung, SK hynix, Micron for 2027.
Any new US export rules on China tools.
FCF conversion back above 90% as receivables unwind.
Glossary
WFE
Wafer fab equipment: the machines used to process silicon wafers into chips; the market Lam sells into.
Etch / deposition
Deposition lays down a thin layer of material; etch removes it in a precise pattern. Repeated hundreds of times per chip.
CSBG
Customer Support Business Group: Lam's spares, service, upgrades and refurbished-tool business.
FCF conversion
Free cash flow / net profit. Above ~90% means profits turn into cash.
ROIC
Return on invested capital: after-tax operating profit / (equity + debt - cash).
DuPont ROE
Net margin x asset turnover x equity multiplier (assets / equity).
PEG
Forward P/E divided by expected EPS growth (%). Below 1 looks cheap, but misleads at cyclical peaks.
EV/EBITDA
Enterprise value (market cap + debt - cash) / EBITDA (operating profit + depreciation and amortisation).
