Takeaways

1

Business overview

What does it do and how did it get here?

HOW IT MAKES MONEY

Advertisers (mostly mobile game studios, increasingly e-commerce brands) set a return-on-ad-spend target in Axon Ads Manager. AppLovin's AI engine, Axon, bids for ad slots across thousands of apps that use its MAX mediation auction, and keeps a cut of every winning ad. Revenue is booked as the platform's take, so gross margin is about 88%.

Since the Apps (own games) business was sold to Tripledot on 30 Jun 2025, AppLovin is a pure advertising company with fewer than 900 employees.

TIMELINE

2012

Founded in Palo Alto by Adam Foroughi, John Krystynak and Andrew Karam.

Aug 2018

KKR buys a minority stake for $400M.

2020–21

Buys game studios (Machine Zone) and measurement firm Adjust.

Apr 2021

IPO on Nasdaq, valued near $24B.

Jan 2022

Closes $1.05B purchase of Twitter's MoPub; Aug 2022 bid for Unity rejected.

2023–24

Axon upgrade drives an inflection: ad revenue +75% in 2024.

Jun 2025

Apps business sold to Tripledot ($400M cash + 20% stake).

Sep 2025

Joins the S&P 500.

2026

Revenue +53% in Q2 but two ~20% earnings-day drops; shares near 52-week low in Oct.

A software marketplace with one product that matters: the Axon model. Revenue per employee is above $7M, which tells you how little labour the machine needs.

2

Moat

Why does it earn its returns, and can rivals copy it?

REAL ADVANTAGES

Data loop. MAX runs the ad auction inside a large share of mobile games, so Axon sees bids, installs and in-app purchases at a scale few rivals can match. Better predictions win more auctions, which brings more data.

Two-sided network. Publishers use MAX because it pays most; advertisers come because the supply is there.

Measured on outcomes. Advertisers buy a ROAS target, so switching is easy only if a rival proves better returns.

WHERE IT IS WEAKER

Model gains come in steps; Q2 2026 growth slowed when an update (the gen-AI video tool) slipped.

Business overview
What does it do and how did it get here?
HOW IT MAKES MONEY

Advertisers (mostly mobile game studios, increasingly e-commerce brands) set a return-on-ad-spend target in Axon Ads Manager. AppLovin's AI engine, Axon, bids for ad slots across thousands of apps that use its MAX mediation auction, and keeps a cut of every winning ad. Revenue is booked as the platform's take, so gross margin is about 88%.

Since the Apps (own games) business was sold to Tripledot on 30 Jun 2025, AppLovin is a pure advertising company with fewer than 900 employees.

TIMELINE
2012
Founded in Palo Alto by Adam Foroughi, John Krystynak and Andrew Karam.
Aug 2018
KKR buys a minority stake for $400M.
2020–21
Buys game studios (Machine Zone) and measurement firm Adjust.
Apr 2021
IPO on Nasdaq, valued near $24B.
Jan 2022
Closes $1.05B purchase of Twitter's MoPub; Aug 2022 bid for Unity rejected.
2023–24
Axon upgrade drives an inflection: ad revenue +75% in 2024.
Jun 2025
Apps business sold to Tripledot ($400M cash + 20% stake).
Sep 2025
Joins the S&P 500.
2026
Revenue +53% in Q2 but two ~20% earnings-day drops; shares near 52-week low in Oct.

A software marketplace with one product that matters: the Axon model. Revenue per employee is above $7M, which tells you how little labour the machine needs.

Data loop. MAX runs the ad auction inside a large share of mobile games, so Axon sees bids, installs and in-app purchases at a scale few rivals can match. Better predictions win more auctions, which brings more data.
Two-sided network. Publishers use MAX because it pays most; advertisers come because the supply is there.
Measured on outcomes. Advertisers buy a ROAS target, so switching is easy only if a rival proves better returns.

E-commerce is a new arena where Meta and Google own the incumbent data and creative tools.

The moat is real in mobile gaming, visible in 80%+ EBITDA margins that competitors with similar products (Unity) cannot get near. It is unproven outside games, and that is where the valuation debate sits.

Source: Arm Holdings ER101 (2026-10-21) · open in site

EQUITY RESEARCH 101 · FIRST-PRINCIPLES OVERVIEW

Arm Holdings plc

Ticker Nasdaq: ARM

Price $221.06 (20 Oct 2026 close)

Mkt cap $236.1bn

EV $232.7bn

Currency USD

FY ends 31 March

Arm designs the CPU blueprints inside most smartphones and a fast-growing share of data-center servers, and gets paid twice: an upfront licence fee and a royalty on every chip shipped. In 2026 it also started selling its own server chip. The business is excellent; the price already assumes years of 25 to 30% growth.

BUSINESS QUALITY

High, with a twist

Ecosystem lock-in and ~98% gross margins. GAAP margins are depressed by stock pay (21% of revenue).

VALUATION

Very rich

~227x trailing GAAP P/E, ~99x FY27E adjusted EPS. Above every chip and EDA peer.

MAIN RISK

Expectations

Royalty growth guided down to high teens; own-chip push adds lower-margin revenue and licensee friction.

CONSENSUS

Buy, PT $291

43 analysts; avg target ~32% above price, range $125 to $500.

01

What does Arm do, and how did it get here?

Arm does not make phones or (until 2026) chips. It designs instruction-set architecture (ISA), CPU cores and pre-integrated compute subsystems (CSS), then licenses them to chipmakers such as Apple, Qualcomm, MediaTek, Nvidia, Amazon and Google. Arm technology has shipped in more than 350 billion chips. In March 2026 it launched the Arm AGI CPU, its first own-brand data-center processor, with Meta as launch customer.

How it makes money

Licensing (47% of FY26 revenue, $2.31bn): upfront fees for access to designs, increasingly via subscription-style Arm Total Access (56 licensees) and Arm Flexible Access (329).

Royalties (53%, $2.61bn): a per-chip fee, usually a % of chip price, paid for years after a design ships. Newer Armv9 and CSS designs carry higher rates.

Silicon (new): selling the AGI CPU directly. Demand cited above $2bn across FY27 and FY28; first-generation gross margin guided high-30s to low-40s%, versus ~98% on IP.

Revenue mix, FY26 ($4,920m)

$2,613m · 53.1%

Licence & other

$2,307m · 46.9%

Timeline

1990

Founded as a joint venture of Acorn, Apple and VLSI.

1993

Apple Newton flops; Arm adopts the licence-plus-royalty model.

1998

Lists in London and on Nasdaq; Nokia phones make Arm the mobile standard.

2016

SoftBank buys Arm for about $32bn and takes it private.

2020-22

Nvidia's planned $40bn purchase collapses on regulatory pushback; Rene Haas becomes CEO (Feb 2022).

Sep 2023

Re-IPO on Nasdaq at $51, valued at $54.5bn.

Mar 2026

Launches the AGI CPU, its first own chip.

Oct 2026

Shares $221; market cap ~$236bn.

02

Why does it earn its returns, and can anyone copy it?

Software ecosystem lock-in. Android, iOS and a growing share of cloud software are compiled for the Arm ISA. Switching to another ISA means re-porting operating systems, toolchains and apps, which costs licensees years.

Neutral standard with scale economics. Arm spreads one R&D budget across hundreds of licensees, so each pays less than designing a core in-house. Its claimed CPU share among top hyperscalers is about 50%.

Power efficiency. Arm cores won mobile on performance per watt; the same logic now drives data-center adoption as power, not chips, limits AI build-outs.

Pricing power through design generations. Armv9 and CSS raise the royalty per chip without needing more units.

Threats to the moat: RISC-V is a free, open ISA; Qualcomm won its Delaware licensing case against Arm (Oct 2025, Arm appealing); selling its own chip turns Arm into a competitor of some customers.

READReal and durable: ~98% gross margin and royalties paid for years after a design ships are the signature of a toll road. The open question is new: whether making its own silicon erodes the neutrality that made licensees trust Arm.

03

What is revenue made of, and which KPIs move it?

Royalty revenue = chips shipped × chip price × royalty rate. Arm cannot control units (phones are flat, servers are growing), so the lever is rate: each move from Armv8 to Armv9 to CSS lifts the royalty per chip. Licensing revenue is lumpy and follows big contract signings; annualized contract value (ACV) smooths it. Silicon adds a third line from FY27.

05

Ratios: leverage, efficiency, returns

RATIO FY22 FY23 FY24 FY25 FY26

READNet cash in every year, so leverage is not a question. ROE of ~11% is low for a toll road because equity is inflated by $1.6bn goodwill and $3.6bn idle cash, and GAAP profit is cut by stock pay. ROIC of ~14% (or roughly 30% on adjusted EBIT) is the better gauge; it fell from FY25 as capex ramped. (ROIC assumes a 20% tax rate.)

06

What is the market paying?

MULTIPLE (TTM TO 30 JUN 2026) VALUE

P/E, trailing GAAP 227.0x

P/E, FY27E adjusted EPS $2.23 99.1x

P/E, FY28E adjusted EPS $3.06 72.2x

Price / FCF, trailing 156.4x

OWN HISTORY P/E EV/EBITDA EV/SALES

Now (20 Oct 26) 227.0x 219.5x 45.1x

READArm is more expensive than at any fiscal year-end since the re-IPO except FY24, when GAAP earnings were crushed by IPO stock awards. A PEG above 3 means the market pays a premium even after crediting the 30%+ expected EPS growth. Forward multiples use adjusted EPS, which excludes stock pay, so the true gap to GAAP is larger.

07

Industry and peers

Arm sells into every compute market: smartphones (mature, units flat, value rising with each chip generation), PCs, autos, IoT and data centers. Data centers are the growth engine: one industry estimate puts the data-center CPU market at $76.6bn by 2029, growing about 35% a year, as AI agents need general-purpose CPUs next to accelerators. Management targets $15bn of total revenue by FY31, about 3x FY26.

READArm trades at roughly 8x Nvidia's trailing earnings multiple despite a lower operating margin and ROIC. Only AMD comes close on trailing P/E. Even on forward adjusted EPS (~99x) Arm is twice AMD and three to four times the EDA software peers, the closest business-model analogues. Peer data as of 20 Oct 2026 close; all multiples trailing GAAP except forward P/E (consensus).

08

Who runs it, and how do they allocate capital?

Rene Haas, CEO since Feb 2022. Took over after the Nvidia deal collapsed, led the 2023 re-IPO and the push into CSS and own silicon. Also on SoftBank's board and part-time CEO of SoftBank Group International since April 2026.

Pay: $60.6m total pay in FY26. A proposed one-off award of 425,000 PSUs, worth up to ~$800m, vests if Arm reaches $1tn, $1.5tn and $2tn market cap by March 2029, 2030 and 2031. ISS and Glass Lewis advised against it; SoftBank's 86% vote controls the outcome.

Ownership: SoftBank owns ~86%, chaired by Masayoshi Son. Insiders hold ~0.06%; free float is small. SoftBank raised a margin loan backed by its Arm shares to $25bn in September 2026.

Capital allocation: no dividend, no open-market buyback. Cash goes to R&D, a step-up in capex for silicon and compute ($545m in FY26 vs $219m), and net-settling employee shares ($529m withholding tax in FY26). Cash and short-term investments: $3.6bn, no financial debt.

READManagement has executed well on growth, but governance is the weak spot for minority holders: a controlling parent that is also a licensing customer, a CEO with dual roles, and a pay plan tied to market cap milestones rather than per-share returns.

09

What would break the story?

HIGH

Valuation leaves no room. At ~227x trailing GAAP earnings, a slowdown from 25-30% growth to mid-teens could cut the multiple in half without any fall in profits.

HIGH

Channel conflict from own silicon. The AGI CPU competes with chips built by licensees (Nvidia Vera, hyperscaler custom CPUs). If customers hedge toward RISC-V, the royalty base erodes. Silicon also dilutes margins (high-30s to low-40s% gross).

MEDIUM

Smartphone squeeze. Memory cost inflation is hurting handset demand; FY27 royalty growth guide already cut to high teens.

MEDIUM

Controlling shareholder. SoftBank (86%) is the largest related-party licensing customer ($193m in Q1 FY27) and has a $25bn margin loan secured on Arm shares. A forced sale or block placement would hit the price.

MEDIUM

Earnings quality. Stock pay of $1.05bn (21% of revenue) separates GAAP EPS ($0.85) from adjusted ($1.77). Receivables of $2.3bn equal ~169 days of revenue.

MEDIUM

Legal and RISC-V. Arm lost its licensing case against Qualcomm in Delaware (appeal pending; Qualcomm's countersuit continues). RISC-V offers a royalty-free alternative.

10

Bear, base, bull

Twelve-month illustrations on FY28 (year to March 2028) adjusted EPS, using consensus as the base. The values are my own estimates; edit them to test your view.

BASE

$291

+31.5% vs $221.06

FY28E adj. EPS ($)

P/E multiple (x)

Consensus: revenue $6.1bn FY27, EPS $2.23 then $3.06

Data-center royalties keep roughly doubling

Multiple holds near today's forward level

AGI CPU above $2bn across FY27 to FY28 at ~45% gross margin

Armv9 and CSS mix lift royalty rates faster

Market prices the $15bn FY31 target as credible

READConsensus average target ($291, 43 analysts, range $125 to $500) sits at the base case. The bear case roughly matches the lowest target, so the downside if growth disappoints (about -43%) is larger than the upside to consensus (about +32%); only the bull case pays clearly more than it risks.

11

Takeaways and what to check next

Remember

Arm is a toll road on computing: ~98% gross margin, royalties paid for years, and lock-in through software.

GAAP profit is a fraction of adjusted profit because of stock pay; judge it on FCF ($1.5bn TTM) and per-share dilution.

Growth has moved from phones to servers, and from pure IP to selling chips, which changes margins and customer relationships.

At ~$236bn, even hitting the $15bn FY31 revenue target at a 35-40% net margin would leave the stock on ~40-45x FY31 earnings. The price already assumes success.

Check next

Q2 FY27 results on 4 Nov 2026: royalty growth vs low-teens guide, licensing vs ~30%, and the promised AGI CPU detail (due with Q3).

Share of licensing revenue from SoftBank over time.

Any licensee announcing a RISC-V server or phone CPU.

Qualcomm appeal and countersuit outcomes.

SoftBank margin-loan terms and any secondary sale of Arm shares.

Glossary

ISA

Instruction-set architecture: the vocabulary of commands software uses to talk to a CPU.

CSS

Compute subsystem: Arm's pre-integrated block of cores, interconnect and memory logic; carries higher royalties.

ACV

Annualized contract value of licence agreements; a smoother gauge of licensing than quarterly revenue.

SBC

Share-based compensation: employee pay in stock; a real cost excluded from adjusted earnings.

ROIC

Return on invested capital: after-tax operating profit ÷ (equity + debt − cash).

PEG

P/E divided by expected EPS growth rate (%). Around 1 is considered fair for growth.

Definitions: EBITDA = GAAP operating income + D&A; debt = lease liabilities (Arm has no borrowings); capex = purchases of PP&E (FY26 excludes $30m of intangibles); forward EPS is adjusted consensus. Scenario values are the author's estimates.

06
What is the market paying?

07
Industry and peers

Arm sells into every compute market: smartphones (mature, units flat, value rising with each chip generation), PCs, autos, IoT and data centers. Data centers are the growth engine: one industry estimate puts the data-center CPU market at $76.6bn by 2029, growing about 35% a year, as AI agents need general-purpose CPUs next to accelerators. Management targets $15bn of total revenue by FY31, about 3x FY26.

READArm trades at roughly 8x Nvidia's trailing earnings multiple despite a lower operating margin and ROIC. Only AMD comes close on trailing P/E. Even on forward adjusted EPS (~99x) Arm is twice AMD and three to four times the EDA software peers, the closest business-model analogues. Peer data as of 20 Oct 2026 close; all multiples trailing GAAP except forward P/E (consensus).

08
Who runs it, and how do they allocate capital?
Rene Haas, CEO since Feb 2022. Took over after the Nvidia deal collapsed, led the 2023 re-IPO and the push into CSS and own silicon. Also on SoftBank's board and part-time CEO of SoftBank Group International since April 2026.
Pay: $60.6m total pay in FY26. A proposed one-off award of 425,000 PSUs, worth up to ~$800m, vests if Arm reaches $1tn, $1.5tn and $2tn market cap by March 2029, 2030 and 2031. ISS and Glass Lewis advised against it; SoftBank's 86% vote controls the outcome.
Ownership: SoftBank owns ~86%, chaired by Masayoshi Son. Insiders hold ~0.06%; free float is small. SoftBank raised a margin loan backed by its Arm shares to $25bn in September 2026.
Capital allocation: no dividend, no open-market buyback. Cash goes to R&D, a step-up in capex for silicon and compute ($545m in FY26 vs $219m), and net-settling employee shares ($529m withholding tax in FY26). Cash and short-term investments: $3.6bn, no financial debt.

READManagement has executed well on growth, but governance is the weak spot for minority holders: a controlling parent that is also a licensing customer, a CEO with dual roles, and a pay plan tied to market cap milestones rather than per-share returns.

09
What would break the story?
HIGH
Valuation leaves no room. At ~227x trailing GAAP earnings, a slowdown from 25-30% growth to mid-teens could cut the multiple in half without any fall in profits.
HIGH
Channel conflict from own silicon. The AGI CPU competes with chips built by licensees (Nvidia Vera, hyperscaler custom CPUs). If customers hedge toward RISC-V, the royalty base erodes. Silicon also dilutes margins (high-30s to low-40s% gross).
MEDIUM
Smartphone squeeze. Memory cost inflation is hurting handset demand; FY27 royalty growth guide already cut to high teens.
MEDIUM
Controlling shareholder. SoftBank (86%) is the largest related-party licensing customer ($193m in Q1 FY27) and has a $25bn margin loan secured on Arm shares. A forced sale or block placement would hit the price.
MEDIUM
Earnings quality. Stock pay of $1.05bn (21% of revenue) separates GAAP EPS ($0.85) from adjusted ($1.77). Receivables of $2.3bn equal ~169 days of revenue.
MEDIUM
Legal and RISC-V. Arm lost its licensing case against Qualcomm in Delaware (appeal pending; Qualcomm's countersuit continues). RISC-V offers a royalty-free alternative.
10
Bear, base, bull

Twelve-month illustrations on FY28 (year to March 2028) adjusted EPS, using consensus as the base. The values are my own estimates; edit them to test your view.

-43.5% vs $221.06

BASE

+31.5% vs $221.06

P/E multiple (x)
Consensus: revenue $6.1bn FY27, EPS $2.23 then $3.06

READConsensus average target ($291, 43 analysts, range $125 to $500) sits at the base case. The bear case roughly matches the lowest target, so the downside if growth disappoints (about -43%) is larger than the upside to consensus (about +32%); only the bull case pays clearly more than it risks.

11
Takeaways and what to check next
Remember
Arm is a toll road on computing: ~98% gross margin, royalties paid for years, and lock-in through software.
GAAP profit is a fraction of adjusted profit because of stock pay; judge it on FCF ($1.5bn TTM) and per-share dilution.
Growth has moved from phones to servers, and from pure IP to selling chips, which changes margins and customer relationships.
At ~$236bn, even hitting the $15bn FY31 revenue target at a 35-40% net margin would leave the stock on ~40-45x FY31 earnings. The price already assumes success.
Check next
Q2 FY27 results on 4 Nov 2026: royalty growth vs low-teens guide, licensing vs ~30%, and the promised AGI CPU detail (due with Q3).
Share of licensing revenue from SoftBank over time.
Any licensee announcing a RISC-V server or phone CPU.
Qualcomm appeal and countersuit outcomes.
SoftBank margin-loan terms and any secondary sale of Arm shares.
Glossary
ISA
Instruction-set architecture: the vocabulary of commands software uses to talk to a CPU.
CSS
Compute subsystem: Arm's pre-integrated block of cores, interconnect and memory logic; carries higher royalties.
ACV
Annualized contract value of licence agreements; a smoother gauge of licensing than quarterly revenue.
SBC
Share-based compensation: employee pay in stock; a real cost excluded from adjusted earnings.
ROIC
Return on invested capital: after-tax operating profit ÷ (equity + debt − cash).
PEG
P/E divided by expected EPS growth rate (%). Around 1 is considered fair for growth.

Monolithic Power Systems

A fabless designer of power-management chips and modules that turn a board's raw supply into the exact voltages a processor, sensor or motor needs. Founded in 1997, it now sells 4,000+ parts across 13 product lines, and AI servers have become its largest end market.

01

Business overview

What does it do and how does it make money?

Every chip in a server, car or phone needs clean, stable power at a precise voltage. MPS designs the integrated circuits and modules that do that conversion (DC/DC converters, power modules, motor drivers, battery and lighting controllers). It is fabless: it designs the silicon and outsources wafer production and assembly, much of it in Asia.

Model: sells thousands of low-ticket parts, mostly through distributors, into six end markets. Pricing power comes from design wins: once a part is designed into a board, it usually ships for that product's life. In Q2 2026 Enterprise Data (AI and server power) was 38.8% of revenue, up from about 22% a year earlier.

Management describes the shift as moving from "chip-only" supplier to a full-service solutions provider (modules, reference designs, software).

1997

Founded by Michael Hsing, an analog process engineer, who still runs it.

Record Q2 revenue $981m; capacity goal "significantly beyond $6bn"; buyback authorisation raised to $1bn.

Named in Vicor's ITC patent complaint on vertical power delivery.

A mature analog franchise that has turned into an AI-infrastructure growth story in under three years. That changes both its growth rate and its risk profile.

02

Moat

Why does it earn its returns, and can rivals copy it?

Process and packaging know-how. MPS develops its own power process technology and runs it at partner foundries. This is why it can sell analog parts at ~55% gross margin without owning fabs, and why ROIC (32.0% TTM) beats fab-owning TI and ADI.

Design-in stickiness. Power stages are qualified with each board; switching costs a redesign. Over 1,500 new automotive sockets shipped in H1 2026 alone.

Speed in high-current AI power. Early leadership in accelerator power for top AI platforms, which competitors (Infineon, Renesas, Vicor, TI) are contesting.

Where it is weaker: no captive fabs (supply depends on partners), heavy China manufacturing exposure, and in AI a few very large customers can shift share fast (a Nov 2024 report of a lost Nvidia socket hit the stock before being disputed).

Returns are durable in the broad catalogue (auto, industrial, storage). In AI, the moat is speed and execution rather than lock-in, so share must be re-won each platform generation.

Industry and competitors

Is the market growing, and how does MPWR compare?

Power management is a large, fragmented analog market. The fastest-growing pocket is AI data-center power, driven by accelerators drawing more current each generation and the move to 48V and 800V rack architectures. Who runs it, and how do they allocate capital?

Michael Hsing, founder, Chairman and CEO since 1997 (29 years). Holds about 964k shares (~2.0% of the company, ~$1.2bn at today's price). Insider transactions over 5 years are all sales, including 30,000 shares on 28 Sep 2026.

Bernie Blegen, EVP and CFO. Signed the Feb 2026 restatement filing; no CFO change reported.

Plan: become a solutions provider, add end markets (800V data-center AC-DC, DDR5 memory power), and diversify the supply chain with capacity well beyond $6bn.

Capital allocation: dividend $8.00/share a year (~45.8% of FY25 GAAP profit); opportunistic buybacks ($636m in 2024, little since; authorisation now $1bn); minimal M&A. Capex is rising to fund capacity.

Incentives: part of executive equity vests on relative TSR vs the PHLX Semiconductor index (75th percentile for maximum); 2026 awards are also tied to securing capacity.

A founder-led company with a long record of compounding and conservative balance sheet. The 2026 restatement and unremediated material weakness are a governance blemish to watch, and steady insider selling means insiders are not adding at these prices.

What would break the story?

MediumChina and trade policy. Heavy reliance on China-based manufacturing; tariffs and export controls are named risks.

MediumCash conversion and inventory. FCF margin down to 17.9% TTM; inventory $676m. Distribution channel inventory can hide a slowdown.

What to remember and what to check next

Monolithic Power Systems

A fabless designer of power-management chips and modules that turn a board's raw supply into the exact voltages a processor, sensor or motor needs. Founded in 1997, it now sells 4,000+ parts across 13 product lines, and AI servers have become its largest end market.

01
Business overview
What does it do and how does it make money?

Every chip in a server, car or phone needs clean, stable power at a precise voltage. MPS designs the integrated circuits and modules that do that conversion (DC/DC converters, power modules, motor drivers, battery and lighting controllers). It is fabless: it designs the silicon and outsources wafer production and assembly, much of it in Asia.

Model: sells thousands of low-ticket parts, mostly through distributors, into six end markets. Pricing power comes from design wins: once a part is designed into a board, it usually ships for that product's life. In Q2 2026 Enterprise Data (AI and server power) was 38.8% of revenue, up from about 22% a year earlier.

Management describes the shift as moving from "chip-only" supplier to a full-service solutions provider (modules, reference designs, software).

Oct 2026

A mature analog franchise that has turned into an AI-infrastructure growth story in under three years. That changes both its growth rate and its risk profile.

02
Moat
Why does it earn its returns, and can rivals copy it?
Process and packaging know-how. MPS develops its own power process technology and runs it at partner foundries. This is why it can sell analog parts at ~55% gross margin without owning fabs, and why ROIC (32.0% TTM) beats fab-owning TI and ADI.
Design-in stickiness. Power stages are qualified with each board; switching costs a redesign. Over 1,500 new automotive sockets shipped in H1 2026 alone.
Speed in high-current AI power. Early leadership in accelerator power for top AI platforms, which competitors (Infineon, Renesas, Vicor, TI) are contesting.
Where it is weaker: no captive fabs (supply depends on partners), heavy China manufacturing exposure, and in AI a few very large customers can shift share fast (a Nov 2024 report of a lost Nvidia socket hit the stock before being disputed).

Returns are durable in the broad catalogue (auto, industrial, storage). In AI, the moat is speed and execution rather than lock-in, so share must be re-won each platform generation.

Is the market growing, and how does MPWR compare?

Who runs it, and how do they allocate capital?
Michael Hsing, founder, Chairman and CEO since 1997 (29 years). Holds about 964k shares (~2.0% of the company, ~$1.2bn at today's price). Insider transactions over 5 years are all sales, including 30,000 shares on 28 Sep 2026.
Bernie Blegen, EVP and CFO. Signed the Feb 2026 restatement filing; no CFO change reported.
Plan: become a solutions provider, add end markets (800V data-center AC-DC, DDR5 memory power), and diversify the supply chain with capacity well beyond $6bn.
Capital allocation: dividend $8.00/share a year (~45.8% of FY25 GAAP profit); opportunistic buybacks ($636m in 2024, little since; authorisation now $1bn); minimal M&A. Capex is rising to fund capacity.
Incentives: part of executive equity vests on relative TSR vs the PHLX Semiconductor index (75th percentile for maximum); 2026 awards are also tied to securing capacity.

MediumChina and trade policy. Heavy reliance on China-based manufacturing; tariffs and export controls are named risks.
MediumCash conversion and inventory. FCF margin down to 17.9% TTM; inventory $676m. Distribution channel inventory can hide a slowdown.

A pre-commercial infrastructure bet. AST has the partner list (60+ carriers, ~3 billion subscribers), $1.3bn of contracted revenue and >$3.7bn of pro forma liquidity, but only 13 of the ~45-60 satellites it needs for continuous service. At ~$17bn EV the market is paying for a working network in 2027, while a launch failure in April, Falcon 9 dependence and SpaceX's spectrum land-grab have halved the stock in a year. Consensus sits at Hold with targets of $42.50 to $108.

The one number that gates the story

How many BlueBirds are in orbit?

In orbit (13)

Commercial US service was tied to roughly 45 satellites in orbit; management now targets that by early 2027, after the April 2026 loss of BlueBird 7. About 25 satellites give intermittent US coverage, 45-60 give continuous coverage in core markets, and about 90 give full global coverage. Every revenue line on this page scales with this bar.

1. Business overview

What does it do, how does it make money, how did it get here?

What it does

AST builds and operates very large low-Earth-orbit satellites (BlueBirds) that act as cell towers in space. They connect directly to ordinary, unmodified smartphones using spectrum lent by mobile carriers plus spectrum AST controls, so a phone keeps 4G/5G voice and data where no ground tower reaches. Headquarters: Midland, Texas.

How it makes money

Wholesale to carriers. AST does not sell to consumers; it partners with mobile network operators (MNOs), who bill their own customers and share the revenue. Terms are not public. Today revenue comes from two other sources: ground gateway equipment sold to MNO partners (Q2 2026 product revenue $24.4m) and US government contracts and milestones (services $7.1m). Government awards total over $125m.

Timeline

May 2017

Abel Avellan founds AST & Science LLC.

Apr 2019

BlueWalker 1 test satellite launches on India's PSLV.

Mar 2020

$110m Series B led by Vodafone and Rakuten, with American Tower and Samsung Next.

Apr 2021

Lists on Nasdaq via merger with New Providence Acquisition Corp.

Sep 2022

BlueWalker 3 prototype launches on Falcon 9; NanoAvionics stake sold to Kongsberg.

Apr 2023

First two-way call between unmodified smartphones via satellite; first space-based 5G call later that year.

Jan-May 2024

AT&T and Google investment; Verizon $100m partnership.

Sep 2024

BlueBirds 1-5 (Block 1) launch together on Falcon 9.

Jun 2025

Ligado deal: up to 45 MHz of North American L-band spectrum to 2107.

Dec 2025

BlueBird 6, first Block 2 satellite, launches on India's LVM3.

Apr 2026

BlueBird 7 on New Glenn reaches too low an orbit and is de-orbited; $125.9m write-off.

Jun-Aug 2026

BlueBirds 8-13 launch on Falcon 9, six in 50 days; 13 in orbit. $1.15bn convertible raised.

Oct 2026

Piper downgrade to Neutral, Deutsche Bank upgrade to Buy; SpaceX buys Grain spectrum; BB14-16 at the Cape.

Nine years in, AST has proved the physics (first call between unmodified phones via satellite in 2023) but not yet the business. 2025 was the year it raised serious money and started mass production; 2026 was meant to be the launch ramp and instead brought a lost satellite and a slipped commercial date.

2. Moat

Why would it earn returns, and can others copy it?

What protects it

Carrier network: 60+ MNO agreements covering ~3 billion subscribers; AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten, Google and American Tower are investors or strategic partners.

Spectrum: up to 45 MHz of L-band and 1670-1675 MHz in North America via Ligado, with rights running to 2107, targeting ~100 MHz in the US and 60+ MHz globally when combined with partner spectrum.

Technology lead in big phased arrays: the BlueBird antenna is the largest commercial LEO array deployed; Block 1 has shown nearly 100 Mbps and Block 2 targets ~200 Mbps peak to standard phones.

Neutral-host position: AST partners with carriers rather than competing with them, which matters more now that SpaceX is building its own carrier.

What erodes it

SpaceX is vertically integrated: its own launch, ~660 direct-to-cell satellites in orbit by early 2026, ~$17bn plus $2.6bn of EchoStar spectrum and an ~$8bn 800 MHz deal with Grain (Oct 2026), plus a 15,000-satellite direct-to-device authorization.

AST depends on SpaceX's Falcon 9 for launch capacity; three BlueBirds fit per Falcon 9 versus up to eight on Blue Origin's New Glenn, which lost BlueBird 7 in April 2026.

The AT&T / Verizon / T-Mobile joint venture explicitly wants several wholesale constellations to buy from. That favors a neutral host but also caps pricing power.

Amazon agreed to buy Globalstar for $11.57bn (Apr 2026), adding a well-funded third D2D entrant.

The moat is real but unfinished: partners and spectrum are hard to copy, the network is not built yet. If AST reaches continuous coverage first and the carrier JV wants a neutral supplier, the position is strong. If launches slip while SpaceX scales, the partner list is only an option.

3. Drivers

What is revenue made of, and which KPIs move it?

Future revenue ≈ (partner subscribers who use satellite service × wholesale price or revenue share) + government contracts + gateway equipment sales. Until ~45 satellites are up, only the last two exist, which is why 2026 revenue (guided at $150-200m) is mostly hardware and government work.

KPI LATEST WHY IT MATTERS

Satellites in orbit 13 (3 more at the Cape) Gates coverage, hence every service dollar. Target ~45 by early 2027.

Launch cadence 6 launched in 50 days (BB8-13) Shows production works; next launch (BB14-16) has no firm date.

Contracted revenue ~$1.3bn Backlog from commercial partners and US government; converts as coverage arrives.

2026 revenue guide $150-200m H1 delivered $46.3m, so H2 needs $104-154m.

Adjusted opex / quarter $119.1m (Q2), up from $91.2m (Q1) The fixed cost base the network must cover.

Liquidity > $3.7bn pro forma (after $1.15bn July convert) Management says enough to build and launch 100+ BlueBirds.

Watch satellites in orbit and launch dates first, then definitive commercial agreements. Revenue in 2026 is a lagging, lumpy signal (Q4 2025 was $54.3m on equipment deliveries, Q1 2026 fell to $14.7m).

9. Risks

What would break the story?

Launch risk and launch access: one satellite already lost (BB7, Apr 2026). AST relies on Falcon 9, built by its main competitor; Piper Sandler flagged that SpaceX could theoretically limit availability.

Schedule slip: commercial launch needs ~45 satellites. BB14-16 have no firm launch date as of mid-October 2026; each quarter of delay is ~$400-500m of burn (estimate from H1 run rate).

Competition: SpaceX now owns spectrum outright and is building its own carrier; Amazon is buying Globalstar. Price competition for wholesale capacity could be fierce.

Dilution and debt: ~$4.1bn of pro forma debt (estimate) and continuing equity issuance; Q2 2026 non-GAAP loss of $0.44/share missed consensus of $0.28.

Regulation: FCC approvals for spectrum and constellation size (Viasat has urged the FCC to reject AST's overseas spectrum bid); the US carrier JV faces DoJ review.

Governance: ~71.6% of votes with the founder; 16.7% of shares sold short, so volatility is high (5-year beta 2.71).

1. Business overview
What does it do, how does it make money, how did it get here?
What it does

AST builds and operates very large low-Earth-orbit satellites (BlueBirds) that act as cell towers in space. They connect directly to ordinary, unmodified smartphones using spectrum lent by mobile carriers plus spectrum AST controls, so a phone keeps 4G/5G voice and data where no ground tower reaches. Headquarters: Midland, Texas.

How it makes money

Wholesale to carriers. AST does not sell to consumers; it partners with mobile network operators (MNOs), who bill their own customers and share the revenue. Terms are not public. Today revenue comes from two other sources: ground gateway equipment sold to MNO partners (Q2 2026 product revenue $24.4m) and US government contracts and milestones (services $7.1m). Government awards total over $125m.

Nine years in, AST has proved the physics (first call between unmodified phones via satellite in 2023) but not yet the business. 2025 was the year it raised serious money and started mass production; 2026 was meant to be the launch ramp and instead brought a lost satellite and a slipped commercial date.

2. Moat
Why would it earn returns, and can others copy it?
What protects it
Carrier network: 60+ MNO agreements covering ~3 billion subscribers; AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, Rakuten, Google and American Tower are investors or strategic partners.
Spectrum: up to 45 MHz of L-band and 1670-1675 MHz in North America via Ligado, with rights running to 2107, targeting ~100 MHz in the US and 60+ MHz globally when combined with partner spectrum.
Technology lead in big phased arrays: the BlueBird antenna is the largest commercial LEO array deployed; Block 1 has shown nearly 100 Mbps and Block 2 targets ~200 Mbps peak to standard phones.
Neutral-host position: AST partners with carriers rather than competing with them, which matters more now that SpaceX is building its own carrier.
What erodes it
SpaceX is vertically integrated: its own launch, ~660 direct-to-cell satellites in orbit by early 2026, ~$17bn plus $2.6bn of EchoStar spectrum and an ~$8bn 800 MHz deal with Grain (Oct 2026), plus a 15,000-satellite direct-to-device authorization.
AST depends on SpaceX's Falcon 9 for launch capacity; three BlueBirds fit per Falcon 9 versus up to eight on Blue Origin's New Glenn, which lost BlueBird 7 in April 2026.
The AT&T / Verizon / T-Mobile joint venture explicitly wants several wholesale constellations to buy from. That favors a neutral host but also caps pricing power.
Amazon agreed to buy Globalstar for $11.57bn (Apr 2026), adding a well-funded third D2D entrant.

The moat is real but unfinished: partners and spectrum are hard to copy, the network is not built yet. If AST reaches continuous coverage first and the carrier JV wants a neutral supplier, the position is strong. If launches slip while SpaceX scales, the partner list is only an option.

3. Drivers
What is revenue made of, and which KPIs move it?

Future revenue ≈ (partner subscribers who use satellite service × wholesale price or revenue share) + government contracts + gateway equipment sales. Until ~45 satellites are up, only the last two exist, which is why 2026 revenue (guided at $150-200m) is mostly hardware and government work.

If AST eventually traded like Iridium, the most profitable listed satellite operator (17.1x EV/EBITDA, 44% EBITDA margin), today's EV would need about $1bn of EBITDA, or roughly $2.3bn of revenue, earned at some future date and discounted back. That is about 20x TTM revenue and 3.9x the 2027 consensus. The ~$1.3bn backlog covers about 57% of one such year. (Calculation, not a forecast.)

P/E, EV/EBITDA and PEG are all negative, so the market is pricing revenue years out. EV/Sales has fallen from 286x at end-2025 to ~147x TTM as revenue arrived and the price fell, and drops to ~29x on 2027 consensus revenue. P/B has come down from 8.5x to ~6.8x. Still far above any operating satellite peer.

7. Industry and competitors
How big can the market get, and who else wants it?

Satellite direct-to-device is early. Kaleido Intelligence (2023) forecast more than $9bn of annual connectivity revenue by 2030; forecasts vary widely. The field has split into vertically integrated players (SpaceX's Starlink, now building a standalone mobile carrier) and carrier-aligned wholesalers (AST, Lynk/Omnispace, Skylo for messaging and IoT), with Amazon entering via Globalstar. The listed peers below are operating satellite businesses, not true D2D comparables; there is no pure-play listed comparable.

COMPANY	MKT CAP	EV	REV TTM $M	EBITDA MARGIN	EV/SALES	EV/EBITDA	FWD P/E	ROIC
AST SpaceMobile ASTS	$16.2bn	$16.9bn	115	n/m	146.6x	n/m	n/m	-15.2%
Iridium IRDM	$4.7bn	$6.7bn	903	44%	7.4x	17.1x	35.5x	6.4%
Viasat VSAT	$8.3bn	$13.5bn	4,630	30%	2.9x	9.7x	537.3x	0.1%
EchoStar ECHO	$25.1bn	$42.2bn	14,650	14%	2.9x	21.2x	32.8x	3.2%
Globalstar* GSAT	$10.8bn	$10.8bn	281	32%	38.3x	118.6x	n/m	3.3%
*Globalstar agreed to be acquired by Amazon for $11.57bn (Apr 2026); its multiples reflect the deal. Peer data trailing, 19-20 Oct 2026. ASTS ROIC uses EBIT before tax over total equity + debt - cash.

Mature satellite operators trade at ~3-7x sales and ~10-21x EBITDA. Globalstar's 38x sales reflects Amazon's pending $11.57bn takeover price, which is the closest public read on what a D2D-capable spectrum-plus-satellite asset is worth. AST's ~147x TTM sales means the market treats it as a growth option rather than an operator.

8. Management
Who runs it, what do they own, how do they allocate capital?
NAME	ROLE	TENURE
Abel Avellan	Founder, Chairman and CEO	Founded AST in 2017; CEO of the listed company since Apr 2021
Scott Wisniewski	President and Chief Strategy Officer	CSO since 2021; President since Jun 2024
Andrew Johnson	EVP, CFO, Chief Legal Officer, Director	CLO since May 2024; CFO since Jun 2024
Shanti Gupta	EVP and Chief Operating Officer	Joined Sep 2021 as CAO; COO since Jun 2024
Dr. Huiwen Yao	Chief Technology Officer	CTO since 2018
Avellan holds all Class C shares: ~78.2m of 389.2m total shares (~20% economic, calculated) but ~71.6% of voting power. Outside shareholders cannot outvote him.
Avellan has taken no base salary beyond minimum-wage requirements since 2021 and no 2025 cash bonus; pay is in RSUs and performance share units (73.75% of 2025 PSUs earned).
Capital allocation is all-in on the network: no dividends, heavy equity and convertible issuance, ~$100m of capital advances to Ligado and $42m of spectrum purchases in H1 2026.
Management targets: ~45 satellites by early 2027, beta service with select MNOs in 2026, commercial launch in 2027, 2026 revenue $150-200m.

A founder-led company with strong alignment through equity and weak outside control through the share structure. The team has hit technical milestones but repeatedly missed timelines (commercial service moved from 2026 to 2027).

9. Risks
What would break the story?
Launch risk and launch access: one satellite already lost (BB7, Apr 2026). AST relies on Falcon 9, built by its main competitor; Piper Sandler flagged that SpaceX could theoretically limit availability.
Schedule slip: commercial launch needs ~45 satellites. BB14-16 have no firm launch date as of mid-October 2026; each quarter of delay is ~$400-500m of burn (estimate from H1 run rate).
Competition: SpaceX now owns spectrum outright and is building its own carrier; Amazon is buying Globalstar. Price competition for wholesale capacity could be fierce.
Dilution and debt: ~$4.1bn of pro forma debt (estimate) and continuing equity issuance; Q2 2026 non-GAAP loss of $0.44/share missed consensus of $0.28.
Regulation: FCC approvals for spectrum and constellation size (Viasat has urged the FCC to reject AST's overseas spectrum bid); the US carrier JV faces DoJ review.
Governance: ~71.6% of votes with the founder; 16.7% of shares sold short, so volatility is high (5-year beta 2.71).
10. Scenarios
Bear, base, bull against the analyst range
Bear
AUTHOR ESTIMATE
$20.00 -52% VS PRICE
Launch cadence slips (Falcon 9 access, no New Glenn), 45 satellites not reached until late 2027 or 2028.
SpaceX wins the US carrier JV's anchor volume; AST's wholesale pricing compresses.
Another large equity raise below today's price; valued near 3x book equity (it traded at 2.5x in 2023).
Base
CONSENSUS AVERAGE
$74.28 +78% VS PRICE
~45 satellites by early 2027 and commercial US service during 2027, as management targets.
Revenue tracks consensus: $167.5m in 2026, ~$582m in 2027.
No further satellite losses; funding holds without heavy new dilution.
Bull
STREET HIGH (S&P PANEL)
$108.00 +159% VS PRICE
60+ satellites through 2027, with New Glenn returning to add capacity.
Carrier JV and major MNOs sign AST as the neutral wholesale network; L-band approved.
Government revenue scales alongside commercial service. (Clear Street's $115 target sits above this panel high.)

Consensus is a Hold with a $74.28 average target, about 78% above the price, and estimates have been cut since Q2 (Zacks: -54.5% revision to the current-quarter EPS consensus). The stock trades just below the lowest Street target of $42.50, so the market is closer to the bear case than analysts are. Street range: low $42.50, median $78, high $108 (13 analysts).

11. Takeaways
What to remember, what to check next
Remember
Satellites in orbit (13 of ~45-60) is the KPI. Everything else follows.
~$17bn EV for $115m of TTM revenue; you are paying for 2027 and beyond.
Funded for now (>$3.7bn pro forma liquidity) but burning ~$2bn a year at H1 2026 pace.
The competitive map changed in 2026: SpaceX owns spectrum, Amazon buys Globalstar, US carriers form a JV that wants multiple suppliers.
Check next
Launch date and outcome for BlueBirds 14-16 on Falcon 9, and any New Glenn return to flight.
Q3 2026 results: revenue versus the $150-200m full-year guide, adjusted opex, and capex run rate.
FCC agenda item dated 29 Oct 2026 on carrier-partner satellite models, and progress on AST's L-band and overseas spectrum filings.
Whether the AT&T / Verizon / T-Mobile JV signs AST as a wholesale supplier, and any definitive (not MoU) agreements converting the 60+ partners.
Diluted share count trend and any further equity or convertible raises.
Glossary
D2D
Direct-to-device: satellites talking straight to an ordinary phone, no special handset or dish.
MNO
Mobile network operator, e.g. AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone.
BlueBird / Block 2
AST's production satellites. Block 2 units are larger, targeting ~200 Mbps peak.
EV/Sales
Enterprise value (market cap + debt - cash) divided by revenue. Used when earnings are negative.
Involuntary conversion
Accounting loss when an asset is destroyed or lost, here BlueBird 7, net of expected insurance.
Noncontrolling interest
Book equity belonging to holders of the operating LLC's units (Class B and C holders) rather than Class A shareholders.
DuPont ROE
Return on equity split into net margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier.
n/m
Not meaningful: the ratio exists arithmetically but says nothing (e.g. margins on near-zero revenue).

Source: CoreWeave ER101 (2026-10-20) · open in site

EQUITY RESEARCH 101 · FIRST-PRINCIPLES OVERVIEW

CoreWeave, Inc.

Nasdaq: CRWV

Price $61.12

Mkt cap $33.7B

EV $79.8B

52-wk $59.51–$141.79

USD · close Oct 19, 2026

BOTTOM LINE

Business: the largest independent "neocloud", renting Nvidia GPU capacity to AI labs and hyperscalers on multi-year take-or-pay contracts. Revenue is compounding at over 100% a year with a $104B backlog.

Quality: not yet a good business on returns. Adjusted ROIC is under 3% while unsecured debt yields approach 15%. Every incremental dollar of growth is debt funded.

Valuation: cheap on forward sales (EV about 6x 2026E revenue), but the equity is a thin slice on top of ~$46B net debt, so small changes in exit multiple swing the share price violently.

Main risk: refinancing and counterparty risk. The story breaks if credit markets close before capex slows and cash flow turns positive.

01

Business overview

CoreWeave builds and runs data centers full of Nvidia GPUs and rents that compute, mostly to train and serve large AI models. Customers sign multi-year contracts for reserved capacity (98% of revenue is committed), often prepaying part of it. CoreWeave uses those contracts as collateral to borrow, buys GPUs, leases powered data-center shells, and earns the spread between contract revenue and the cost of power, depreciation and interest.

How it makes money

Reserved GPU capacity on 2 to 6 year contracts, billed per GPU-hour (the bulk of revenue)

On-demand capacity at higher rates

Software layer: managed Kubernetes, Mission Control, Weights & Biases tooling

Customers: Microsoft (about 67% of 2025 revenue), OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic, plus a growing enterprise list

History

Sep 2017

Founded as Atlantic Crypto in New Jersey, mining Ethereum on GPUs

2019

Renamed CoreWeave after the crypto crash; repurposes GPUs for cloud

2022

Spends ~$100M on Nvidia H100s ahead of the AI boom

Apr 2023

Nvidia invests $100M; Aug: $2.3B GPU-backed debt facility

May 2024

$1.1B raise at ~$19B valuation

Mar 2025

~$12B OpenAI contract; Nasdaq IPO raises $1.5B at $40/share

Oct 2025

Core Scientific holders reject $9B takeover

Jan 2026

Nvidia invests $2B at $87.20/share

Apr 2026

Anthropic deal; $21B Meta expansion; $3.5B converts

Aug 2026

Q2 revenue +112%; backlog $104B; joins Nasdaq-100

Oct 2026

Stock falls ~20% in a week on debt fears

A crypto miner that pivoted at exactly the right moment. Its edge came from buying H100s early and having Nvidia as an investor and supplier. It is now a capital-intensive infrastructure lessor more than a software company.

02

Moat

Real advantages

Speed: first to commercially deploy Nvidia GB300 NVL72 systems; stands up clusters faster than hyperscalers

Priority allocation from Nvidia, which owns about 10.7% of Class A shares and invested $2B in Jan 2026

Purpose-built AI stack and performance tuning that frontier labs value

Contracted power pipeline of 3.7 GW (4.2 GW incl. early Q3 adds); power is the scarce input

Why it may not last

The product (Nvidia GPUs in a building with power) is replicable by Oracle, Nebius, IREN and hyperscalers

Largest customers are also its competitors and are building their own capacity

Cost of capital disadvantage: hyperscalers fund near investment grade rates, CoreWeave at B+

No switching costs once a contract ends; capacity gets re-bid

A time-based edge (speed, allocation, power), not a structural one. It is real today because demand exceeds supply. Whether it survives a balanced market is the central question.

03

Drivers

Revenue ≈ active power (MW) × utilization × revenue per MW. Contracted power converts into active power as sites are energized, and backlog converts into revenue as capacity goes live.

1.5 GW

72%

25%

Net interest / revenue, TTM

The single number to watch is active power: 1.5 GW at Q2 2026 against 3.7 GW contracted. Each delayed megawatt pushes revenue right while debt costs keep running. Revenue per MW is our estimate from Q2 annualized revenue over average active power.

04

Financials

Capital allocation is single-minded: everything goes to capex, funded by debt, converts and equity (Nvidia, Jane Street). No dividends to common holders.

05

Ratios

FY24 FY25 TTM / JUN-26

Net debt incl. leases / adj. EBITDA 7.6x 8.6x 10.5x

Net debt excl. leases / adj. EBITDA 5.4x 5.9x 6.7x

DuPont: × equity multiplier n/m 23.0x n/a

Leverage is 10.5x adjusted EBITDA including leases (6.7x excluding). Adjusted operating income covers interest only 0.2 to 0.5 times. Asset turnover of 0.15x means each dollar of assets earns 15 cents of revenue a year, so returns depend on high margins sustained over the full asset life. DuPont ROE is distorted by tiny book equity.

06

Valuation

METRIC TRAILING (TTM) 2026E 2027E

P/E n/m n/m n/m

EPS (non-GAAP consensus) (3.50) GAAP (3.96) (1.86)

PEG n/m n/m n/m

Price / sales 4.4x 2.6x 1.3x

EV / adj. EBITDA 18.1x n/a n/a

Price vs history -57% vs 52-wk high -30% vs Nvidia's $87.20 +53% vs $40 IPO

P/E and PEG are not meaningful (losses through at least 2027 on consensus). On EV/forward sales CoreWeave trades below Oracle and Nebius. Against its own short history, the stock is 57% off its 52-week high of $141.79, below the $87.20 Nvidia paid in Jan 2026, and above its $40 IPO price.

07

Industry and competitors

AI compute demand is still growing faster than supply; management targets at least 8 GW of active power by 2030. Peers range from cash-rich hyperscalers to other leveraged neoclouds. Trailing metrics, close on Oct 19, 2026; EBITDA as reported by StockAnalysis.

COMPANY MKT CAP $B EV $B REV TTM $B OP MARGIN ROIC NET DEBT / EBITDA FCF $B EV / SALES EV / EBITDA FWD P/S P/E

CoreWeave CRWV 33.7 79.7 7.59 -3.0% -0.3% 12.1x (13.7) 10.5x 21.0x 1.7x n/m

Nebius NBIS 46.7 48.8 1.36 -37.4% -4.1% 8.3x (5.9) 36.0x n/m 6.5x n/m

IREN IREN 10.9 12.9 0.71 -53.6% -7.2% 51.1x (2.2) 18.2x n/m 3.9x n/m

Oracle ORCL 392.9 524.9 71.78 34.3% 11.3% 3.8x (28.7) 7.3x 15.2x 4.0x 20.3x

Microsoft MSFT 3,960 4,010 331.84 46.8% 26.2% 0.3x 67.0 12.1x 20.7x 10.1x 29.7x

CoreWeave is the cheapest neocloud on forward sales and the most levered. Oracle is the closest scaled comparison and also burning cash on AI capex, but it has a profitable legacy business underneath. Microsoft shows what a moated cloud earns: 26% ROIC.

08

Management

Who runs it

Michael Intrator, co-founder and CEO since 2017 (9 years); 38.7% of voting power

Brian Venturo, co-founder, Chief Strategy Officer; 20.3% of votes

Brannin McBee, co-founder, Chief Development Officer; 14.6% of votes, 10b5-1 sale plan from Mar 2026

Nitin Agrawal, CFO since 2024 (ex-Google); Sachin Jain, COO (ex-Oracle)

Governance and allocation

Dual class: Class B carries 10 votes; insiders control ~72% of votes until a 2032 sunset

Plan: 2026 capex $35 to $39B, at least 8 GW active by 2030

Bolt-on software M&A: Weights & Biases, OpenPipe, Monolith AI; the $9B Core Scientific deal was voted down by CORZ holders in Oct 2025

Financing creativity: delayed-draw term loans secured by contracts, converts, a Eurobond

Founder-led with heavy ownership, which aligns incentives on upside but leaves outside shareholders no real vote. Management has consistently chosen growth over balance-sheet safety.

09

Risks

Financial

Refinancing: S&P rating B+; unsecured yields near 15% in Oct 2026; stock fell 20% in the week to Oct 16 on debt fears

Interest burden: $640M in Q2 alone, about 25% of revenue

Dilution: equity raises and converts as capex outruns cash flow

Business

Concentration: top 3 customers ~72% of Q2 revenue; top one ~36%

Counterparty: backlog is only as good as customers' ability to pay, including cash-burning AI labs

Obsolescence: GPU depreciation lives may prove too long if Nvidia's cadence makes older chips uneconomic

Execution and politics: power and construction delays; state moratoria on data centers

These risks compound each other. A delay pushes revenue out, which weakens coverage, which raises the cost of the next financing.

10

Scenarios (12-month view)

Analyst consensus: Buy from 41 analysts; average target $140.58, median $147.50, range $39 to $278. Consensus revenue: $12.9B (2026), $26.3B (2027). The scenarios below are our illustrative estimates, valuing the equity on 2027 revenue less estimated year-end 2026 net debt.

BEAR

$14

-77% vs $61.12 · 3.5x × $20B

Power and build delays cut 2027 revenue to $20B

A key customer trims or re-bids capacity

Credit stress compresses multiple to 3.5x

BASE

$101

65% vs $61.12 · 4.5x × $26.34B

2027 revenue at consensus $26.3B

Financing stays open at current costs

Multiple re-rates modestly to 4.5x as FCF path clears

BULL

$211

245% vs $61.12 · 6x × $30B

Faster energization lifts 2027 revenue to $30B

New investment-grade customers diversify mix

Spreads tighten; multiple moves toward 6x

TRY IT: IMPLIED SHARE PRICE

Bull

Market-implied

2027 revenue ($B)

$26.5B

EV / 2027 sales (x)

4.5x

Net debt YE-26 incl. leases ($B)

$62B

Diluted shares (M)

560M

IMPLIED PRICE

$102

EV $119B − net debt $62B · 67% vs today

Consensus avg target $140.58 · market-implied 3.6x

Today's price implies about 3.6x EV/2027 sales once the debt needed for 2026 capex is counted. The equity behaves like an option: a one-turn change in the multiple moves the price by roughly $45. Consensus targets sit near our base case only if you accept ~4.5x 2027 sales.

11

Takeaways

Remember

Hypergrowth with real contracted demand ($104B backlog plus $25B added early Q3)

Economics today: ~58% adj. EBITDA margin, ~0% GAAP operating margin, ~25% of revenue to interest

Returns on capital far below cost of capital; value depends entirely on the post-buildout steady state

Highly levered equity: outcome range is very wide

Check next (Q3 report, ~Nov 11, 2026)

Active power vs 1.5 GW, and any slippage in energization

2027 capex framework and how it will be funded

Terms of the next debt raise (spread, secured vs unsecured)

Microsoft share of revenue and new investment-grade customers

Depreciation life assumptions and any impairments

Glossary and definitions

A crypto miner that pivoted at exactly the right moment. Its edge came from buying H100s early and having Nvidia as an investor and supplier. It is now a capital-intensive infrastructure lessor more than a software company.

02
Moat
Real advantages
Speed: first to commercially deploy Nvidia GB300 NVL72 systems; stands up clusters faster than hyperscalers
Priority allocation from Nvidia, which owns about 10.7% of Class A shares and invested $2B in Jan 2026
Purpose-built AI stack and performance tuning that frontier labs value
Contracted power pipeline of 3.7 GW (4.2 GW incl. early Q3 adds); power is the scarce input
Why it may not last
The product (Nvidia GPUs in a building with power) is replicable by Oracle, Nebius, IREN and hyperscalers
Largest customers are also its competitors and are building their own capacity
Cost of capital disadvantage: hyperscalers fund near investment grade rates, CoreWeave at B+
No switching costs once a contract ends; capacity gets re-bid

A time-based edge (speed, allocation, power), not a structural one. It is real today because demand exceeds supply. Whether it survives a balanced market is the central question.

Revenue ≈ active power (MW) × utilization × revenue per MW. Contracted power converts into active power as sites are energized, and backlog converts into revenue as capacity goes live.

AI compute demand is still growing faster than supply; management targets at least 8 GW of active power by 2030. Peers range from cash-rich hyperscalers to other leveraged neoclouds. Trailing metrics, close on Oct 19, 2026; EBITDA as reported by StockAnalysis.

CoreWeave is the cheapest neocloud on forward sales and the most levered. Oracle is the closest scaled comparison and also burning cash on AI capex, but it has a profitable legacy business underneath. Microsoft shows what a moated cloud earns: 26% ROIC.

08
Management
Who runs it
Michael Intrator, co-founder and CEO since 2017 (9 years); 38.7% of voting power
Brian Venturo, co-founder, Chief Strategy Officer; 20.3% of votes
Brannin McBee, co-founder, Chief Development Officer; 14.6% of votes, 10b5-1 sale plan from Mar 2026
Nitin Agrawal, CFO since 2024 (ex-Google); Sachin Jain, COO (ex-Oracle)
Governance and allocation
Dual class: Class B carries 10 votes; insiders control ~72% of votes until a 2032 sunset
Plan: 2026 capex $35 to $39B, at least 8 GW active by 2030
Bolt-on software M&A: Weights & Biases, OpenPipe, Monolith AI; the $9B Core Scientific deal was voted down by CORZ holders in Oct 2025
Financing creativity: delayed-draw term loans secured by contracts, converts, a Eurobond

Founder-led with heavy ownership, which aligns incentives on upside but leaves outside shareholders no real vote. Management has consistently chosen growth over balance-sheet safety.

09
Risks
Financial
Refinancing: S&P rating B+; unsecured yields near 15% in Oct 2026; stock fell 20% in the week to Oct 16 on debt fears
Interest burden: $640M in Q2 alone, about 25% of revenue
Dilution: equity raises and converts as capex outruns cash flow
Business
Concentration: top 3 customers ~72% of Q2 revenue; top one ~36%
Counterparty: backlog is only as good as customers' ability to pay, including cash-burning AI labs
Obsolescence: GPU depreciation lives may prove too long if Nvidia's cadence makes older chips uneconomic
Execution and politics: power and construction delays; state moratoria on data centers

These risks compound each other. A delay pushes revenue out, which weakens coverage, which raises the cost of the next financing.

10
Scenarios (12-month view)

Analyst consensus: Buy from 41 analysts; average target $140.58, median $147.50, range $39 to $278. Consensus revenue: $12.9B (2026), $26.3B (2027). The scenarios below are our illustrative estimates, valuing the equity on 2027 revenue less estimated year-end 2026 net debt.

Takeaways

Hypergrowth with real contracted demand ($104B backlog plus $25B added early Q3)

Source: Broadcom AVGO Overview (2026-10-19) · open in site

EQUITY RESEARCH 101 · FIRST-PRINCIPLES OVERVIEW

Broadcom Inc. AVGO

Price $328.75 (16 Oct 2026)

Market cap $1.57T

EV $1.60T

Exchange Nasdaq

Reporting USD, FY ends early Nov

HQ Palo Alto, California

Broadcom is two businesses under one cash-flow machine: custom AI accelerators and networking chips for a handful of hyperscalers and AI labs, and VMware-led infrastructure software. AI has taken revenue from $64B in FY25 to an $89B run over the last four quarters, and the stock now trades about 35% below its peak on fears that its customers cannot fund the build-out.

BUSINESS QUALITY

Exceptional, concentrated

GAAP operating margin 48%, FCF margin 44%, ROIC 27% even with $124B of acquisition goodwill and intangibles in the base.

VALUATION

Cheap if FY27 happens

42.0x trailing GAAP P/E but 16.9x FY27 consensus EPS. Below its FY24–25 multiples and in line with Nvidia and TSMC on forward P/E.

MAIN RISK

Customer funding

Six XPU customers drive 73% of AI revenue, and two of the largest (OpenAI, Anthropic) depend on outside capital. The CEO himself flagged capital as the next constraint.

CONSENSUS

Strong Buy, $528 avg

50 analysts; targets $216–$660. Average implies +60% and sits close to the base case below.

01

What does it do, and how did it get here?

Broadcom designs chips and sells enterprise software; it owns no fabs and has TSMC make its silicon. Semiconductor Solutions (70% of Q3 FY26 revenue) sells custom AI accelerators (XPUs) co-designed with each customer, Ethernet switching and optics for AI clusters, plus legacy lines in broadband, wireless, storage and industrial. Infrastructure Software (30%) is mostly VMware Cloud Foundation sold as subscriptions, plus mainframe, security and other acquired franchises. About 48% of revenue goes through distributors, and the top five end customers were roughly 40% of FY25 revenue.

Timeline

1961

Starts as HP Associates, Hewlett-Packard's semiconductor arm.

1999

Goes with Agilent when HP spins off its test and components businesses.

2005

2019

Buys Symantec's enterprise security unit for $10.7B.

2023

Closes VMware (about $69B incl. debt); HQ moves to Palo Alto.

2025–26

Custom AI chips (XPUs) for Google, Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic become the growth engine.

Broadcom was built by buying franchises with dominant share, cutting costs hard, and harvesting cash. VMware (FY24) lifted software to ~40% of revenue; since then custom AI silicon has flipped the mix back to chips, with AI alone 56% of Q3 FY26 revenue.

02

Why does it earn its returns? (moat)

Custom silicon know-how

Building a hyperscaler's own accelerator needs high-speed SerDes, advanced packaging and memory integration that few firms can supply at scale. Customers co-design over multiple generations (Google TPU, Meta MTIA), so switching mid-roadmap is costly.

Ethernet networking

AI networking grew over 2.5x year on year in Q3 FY26 and management expects it to keep pace with XPUs. Broadcom's switch silicon is the default for open Ethernet AI clusters, the main alternative to Nvidia's proprietary fabric.

Supply and financing scale

Broadcom has locked in lasers, substrates (own Singapore substrate fab from FY27) and memory, and set up XPV with Apollo and Blackstone to help fund 20+ GW of customer compute. Smaller rivals cannot promise that capacity.

Software lock-in

VMware runs the private data centers of most large enterprises. Ripping it out is slow and risky, which lets Broadcom push bundled subscriptions at about 84% segment operating margin.

The moat is real but narrow in customers: it rests on deep, multi-year engineering ties with six XPU buyers who are also the most capable firms on earth at designing chips in-house. Pricing power is strongest in software and networking, weaker on XPUs, where gross margin is already falling.

03

What is revenue made of, and which KPIs move it?

AI revenue = gigawatts of customer compute deployed × Broadcom content per gigawatt (XPUs, switches, optics), split by customer. Software revenue = installed VMware cores × subscription price, which grows as perpetual licences convert. Non-AI chips follow the broadband, enterprise and wireless cycles.

Broadcom grows faster than every peer except Nvidia, with near-Nvidia FCF margins, yet trades at the same forward P/E as Nvidia, TSMC and slow-growing Qualcomm, and at less than half Marvell's or AMD's. The market is applying a concentration and financing discount, not a growth premium.

08

Who runs it?

Hock Tan, President & CEO (since 2006)

Architect of the acquire-cut-harvest model from Avago to VMware. A September 2025 performance award pays over 600,000 shares if AI revenue reaches $90B in any 12 months between FY28 and FY30, roughly tripling above $120B; the board framed it as extending his leadership through FY2030. About 96% of his target pay is variable.

Henry Samueli, Chairman

Co-founder of the original Broadcom Corp., independent chair. The board is running CEO succession planning and shrinks to eight directors in 2026.

Kirsten Spears, CFO

Runs a conservative balance sheet: $59.6B of fixed-rate debt at a ~4% average coupon, $7.1B repaid since Q3 began.

Ownership and allocation

Insiders own about 1.1% of shares (S&P Global). Priorities: dividends that rise yearly, debt paydown after deals, opportunistic buybacks ($8.5B in FY26 to date), and large acquisitions when the price is right.

Twenty years of disciplined capital allocation and pay tied to hard AI-revenue targets align management with owners. Key-person risk is real: the playbook is Tan's, and a successor has not been named.

09

What could break the story?

Customer concentration. AI is 56% of revenue and six XPU customers are 73% of AI. One customer pausing, insourcing or switching to Nvidia or another ASIC house would hit revenue directly.

Customers' ability to pay. Anthropic and OpenAI are set to be the two largest XPU buyers by 2027 and rely on outside funding. Tan said in October 2026 that capital may become AI's next bottleneck, and Broadcom's XPV vehicle could leave it with residual value guarantees.

Margin mix. Gross margin is guided to 73% in Q4 versus 78% a year ago as memory-heavy XPUs grow. If operating margin cannot hold near 66%, EPS lags revenue.

Target credibility. Analysts questioned the revenue per gigawatt implied by the FY27–28 targets (about $11–12B, versus far higher for Nvidia systems). Missing the $115B FY27 target would reset the multiple.

Supply chain and geopolitics. Manufacturing at TSMC in Taiwan, plus tight lasers, substrates and memory. Export controls or a Taiwan disruption would stop shipments.

Software decay. VMware growth is slowing to mid-teens ARR as licence conversions mature, and price increases have pushed some customers to look for alternatives.

EQUITY RESEARCH 101 · FIRST-PRINCIPLES OVERVIEW
Broadcom Inc. AVGO
Price $328.75 (16 Oct 2026)
Market cap $1.57T
EV $1.60T
Exchange Nasdaq
Reporting USD, FY ends early Nov
HQ Palo Alto, California

Broadcom is two businesses under one cash-flow machine: custom AI accelerators and networking chips for a handful of hyperscalers and AI labs, and VMware-led infrastructure software. AI has taken revenue from $64B in FY25 to an $89B run over the last four quarters, and the stock now trades about 35% below its peak on fears that its customers cannot fund the build-out.

BUSINESS QUALITY
Exceptional, concentrated

GAAP operating margin 48%, FCF margin 44%, ROIC 27% even with $124B of acquisition goodwill and intangibles in the base.

VALUATION
Cheap if FY27 happens

42.0x trailing GAAP P/E but 16.9x FY27 consensus EPS. Below its FY24–25 multiples and in line with Nvidia and TSMC on forward P/E.

MAIN RISK
Customer funding

Six XPU customers drive 73% of AI revenue, and two of the largest (OpenAI, Anthropic) depend on outside capital. The CEO himself flagged capital as the next constraint.

CONSENSUS
Strong Buy, $528 avg

50 analysts; targets $216–$660. Average implies +60% and sits close to the base case below.

01
What does it do, and how did it get here?

Broadcom designs chips and sells enterprise software; it owns no fabs and has TSMC make its silicon. Semiconductor Solutions (70% of Q3 FY26 revenue) sells custom AI accelerators (XPUs) co-designed with each customer, Ethernet switching and optics for AI clusters, plus legacy lines in broadband, wireless, storage and industrial. Infrastructure Software (30%) is mostly VMware Cloud Foundation sold as subscriptions, plus mainframe, security and other acquired franchises. About 48% of revenue goes through distributors, and the top five end customers were roughly 40% of FY25 revenue.

Timeline
1961

Starts as HP Associates, Hewlett-Packard's semiconductor arm.

2005

KKR and Silver Lake buy Agilent's chip unit for $2.6B and name it Avago.

Agrees to buy LSI for $6.6B (storage, networking).

2016

2018

2019

Buys Symantec's enterprise security unit for $10.7B.

2023

Closes VMware (about $69B incl. debt); HQ moves to Palo Alto.

2025–26

Custom AI chips (XPUs) for Google, Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic become the growth engine.

Broadcom was built by buying franchises with dominant share, cutting costs hard, and harvesting cash. VMware (FY24) lifted software to ~40% of revenue; since then custom AI silicon has flipped the mix back to chips, with AI alone 56% of Q3 FY26 revenue.

02
Why does it earn its returns? (moat)
Custom silicon know-how

Building a hyperscaler's own accelerator needs high-speed SerDes, advanced packaging and memory integration that few firms can supply at scale. Customers co-design over multiple generations (Google TPU, Meta MTIA), so switching mid-roadmap is costly.

Ethernet networking

AI networking grew over 2.5x year on year in Q3 FY26 and management expects it to keep pace with XPUs. Broadcom's switch silicon is the default for open Ethernet AI clusters, the main alternative to Nvidia's proprietary fabric.

Supply and financing scale

Broadcom has locked in lasers, substrates (own Singapore substrate fab from FY27) and memory, and set up XPV with Apollo and Blackstone to help fund 20+ GW of customer compute. Smaller rivals cannot promise that capacity.

Software lock-in

VMware runs the private data centers of most large enterprises. Ripping it out is slow and risky, which lets Broadcom push bundled subscriptions at about 84% segment operating margin.

The moat is real but narrow in customers: it rests on deep, multi-year engineering ties with six XPU buyers who are also the most capable firms on earth at designing chips in-house. Pricing power is strongest in software and networking, weaker on XPUs, where gross margin is already falling.

03
What is revenue made of, and which KPIs move it?

AI revenue = gigawatts of customer compute deployed × Broadcom content per gigawatt (XPUs, switches, optics), split by customer. Software revenue = installed VMware cores × subscription price, which grows as perpetual licences convert. Non-AI chips follow the broadband, enterprise and wireless cycles.

Verdict: OVERVALUED

Base-case intrinsic value $279.78 per share vs $362.62 at the time of the memo.

What my research says

notes.html:
What my research says

  • Analysis (2026-11-16): Conclusion (historical evidence only). No CAPM window shows statistically significant positive alpha for SNPS at the 5% level using Newey-West HAC inference. Customers are chip designers (Nvidia, AMD, Apple, Qualcomm, hyperscalers) and foundries; contracts are mostly multi-year licences, so 82% of revenue is recurring. open
